subsubtopic: UNIVERSAL ACCESS TO FAIR ORAL HEARINGS BEFORE REFUGEE BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition signed by people from my constituency as well as from other constituencies both within Toronto and, indeed, from as far afield as the Northwest Territories, and Edmonton.
The petitioners point out that the Standing Committee of Parliament has proposed a new procedure for refugee determination which is quicker and fairer than the one now in force and they pray and call upon Parliament to ensure that legislation be enacted which will embody the principles of fair and quick oral hearings of refugee claimants, universal access to such hearings for every claimant in Canada and adequate opportunity to arrive in Canada to make these claims.

subsubtopic: SUPPORT FOR PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO IMMIGRATION ACT,
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 have the honour to present to the House a petition from the residents of Calgary South who call upon the House to pass in full Bills C-55 and C-84. Canadians are law-abiding citizens and the people of Calgary South are very angry and extremely annoyed. They want tough new legislation now to deal with this disastrous situation of bogus claimants entering Canada illegally and of course those people who are trafficking in human bodies. This petition represents the views of my riding on this very important issue.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO TAX ON FOOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my duty to present a petition to the House, signed by constituents from my riding and the National Capital Region, and stating that, whereas since September, 1984, the federal Government has imposed on Canadian taxpayers 25 new taxes
or tax increases, in particular on medical and dental supplies, snack foods, candy and soft drinks; and whereas the federal Government in its tax reform proposal has studied the possiblity of imposing on Canadians a general tax on goods and services, including food; and whereas food constitutes a vital element of day-to-day life; and whereas the imposition of theis tax would have the effect of seriously penalizing certain categories of taxpayers such as the aged, families, the unemployed. low income taxpayers, youth and so forth, your petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to reject all measures that would have the effect of imposing a sales tax on food products.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask that all questions be allowed to stand.

speechtext: Is it agreed?
Agreed.

The House resumed from Monday, August 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard that Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee, and the amendment of Mr. Marchi, (p. 7338).

Mr. Speaker, many well-respected and knowledgeable citizens of Canada and other countries have intimate and expert knowledge of the problems of immigration and refugees. Many of these individuals have made that knowledge and expertise available to the Government. As well, the committees of this House have made representations to the Government on the same subject. Unfortunately, the Government chose to ignore that advice.

August 18, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
In 1985 the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration tabled a report recommending major changes in the refugee determination process. Those changes were fair and would have provided protection under Canadian law and the Charter of Rights for refugees seeking asylum. Instead, the Government brought in Bill C-55 and allowed three days of debate in June. When there was a storm of protest about some of the provisions of the Bill it was left on the shelf. The Government now claims an emergency exists and appears to want it passed without delay or change. It appears to be ignoring its own committees as well as people like Rabbi Gunther Plaut who have expressed concern about this Bill.
Worse than that, the Government is doing its best to confuse Canadians as to who is a legitimate refugee and who is an immigrant. Government Members who have spoken on this Bill have made statements which suggest that refugees are somehow jumping the queue in entering Canada the way they do. In doing so those Members are either ignorant of the procedures for entry into Canada or are deliberately misleading Canadians-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: That is not true at all.
-in order to confuse the issue and make this Bill palatable. Instead of doing that, they should be explaining clearly that there are two queues, two streams-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Four.

-and that the bogus refugee is not replacing a legitimate immigrant under the regular process. The refugee is in a different stream. Whether they get in or not, they do not replace someone in the regular immigrant stream. A bogus refugee, when proven to be such, is excluded and sent back. He does not move over to the head of the immigrant queue. That is the situation and many government Members have tried to confuse the public. It is the process of refugee determination that is the problem.
Canadians generally are generous in their acceptance of refugees in Canada. However, it should not take five years to decide whether or not a person claiming refugee status is a legitimate refugee. The Government, quite rightly, is doing something about the determination process, but what it is doing is unacceptable to most Canadians who understand that it is moving us closer to a totalitarian approach. Most democracies and the UN cannot accept that.
Our history of dealing with refugees started badly. I refer to the Sikhs who tried to enter Canada in 1914 and the Jews who attempted to land in Montreal in 1939. Since then we have improved our image to the point where last year we won an award for our treatment of refugees. Yet we now seem to be moving to again put ourselves in the position where Canada's approach to refugees will be unacceptable to most people in this country and most people around the world. That will happen if the Government passes this Bill in its present form.
The Government has the time and the power to improve the Bill. It will be a sad day for Canada if it does not heed the advice of the experts and concerned individuals and groups who suggest that, although the Bill is needed, it is unacceptable in its present form.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity this morning to take part in the debate on Bill C-55. I must say I would welcome it even more if the Bill were better drafted than what we have here. I hope the parliamentary committee responsible for examining the Bill will be able to amend it and make it more equitable.
Mr. Speaker, some Conservative Members have been using the refugee question in recent months to restore their Government's tarnished image. For instance, in a letter sent by a Conservative Member from the Toronto area to his constituents on July 14, 1987, we read the following, and I quote:

Since my last letter we have witnessed another boatload of refugees land in Canada.
Like you, I am angry. Angry because our government acted responsibly to change the law to prevent another incident like that of the Tamils last summer so that the matter could be resolved expeditiously and fairly.
Bill C-55, which would grant the government the necessary power to curb this type of influx, has been blocked at every turn. It has been thwarted by opposition from both the Liberals and NDP along with a strong lobbying effort being directed by most churches.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Hear, hear!

I notice that the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) says "hear, hear''. It is interesting that he would agree with the ill-conceived and erroneous comments of his colleague, the Member for Etobicoke North (Mr. Pennock), who accuses the Opposition and the churches of the mistakes for which the Government is responsible. Perhaps we in Opposition are fair game for this kind of nonsense perpetrated by the Government. I do not, however, share the "hear, hear" of the Member across when referring to the churches, whether my church, his or anyone else's.
Had the Member for Etobicoke North chosen to tell the truth he would have told his constituents that the number of refugees landing on our shores prior to the Government taking power was not very large per year. In 1985 the number increased to 8,000. That did not happen because the Government was in power. Although I do make my share of partisan remarks, this is not one of them. It is obvious that there has been an influx of refugees because conditions in certain countries are getting worse and people want to come here. In 1986 the number increased to 18,000. I understand that by May, 1987, 10,000 people had already requested refugee status. That is a dramatic increase.
For a Member on the other side to accuse the Opposition or the churches of stalling a Bill which was not even introduced
August 18, 1987

until nearly 10 months after the arrival of the Tamil refugees is somewhat less than honest. As a matter of fact, it is a lot less than honest.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Why are we debating a six-month hoist? Tell us about that.

Let us talk about the truth and the way in which the Government has handled this most unfortunate situation. The Government is desperately trying to cling to power using every available tool, including hitting those who are least able to help themselves; an attempt to restore public confidence in the Government. The Government has made much of the 174 refugees who arrived this year and of the Tamils who arrived last year.
I do not think it is right when people abuse our immigration laws. I know that the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) does not think that is right either. 1 know that the Minister knows better and is not the cause of this, but I disagree with his Leader, who is the cause of this mess, when he tries to perpetrate the kinds of things we saw earlier this year.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) tried to convince Canadians that Parliament had to be recalled for an emergency. Two weeks later no one had gotten around to phoning the Speaker to tell him about the emergency for which the House had to be recalled. At the time he said it was an emergency, the boat had already been here for three weeks. Five weeks elapsed in that time of emergency. The whole purpose of the exercise was obviously to try desperately to have Canadians express confidence in him again. It obviously has not worked. It will not work because it is wrong.
1 am sure the Minister knows that to be the fact, but he is stuck with it as am I as an opposition Member. He cannot say he does not like it, as 1 can, because he is a member of the Cabinet. He did not invent the rule, but he has to put up with it and carry the load and the blame. That is unfair, because I think the Minister is a very fine gentleman, but he has to carry that on his shoulders.
We cannot discuss refugee policy without as well discussing immigration policy generally. We know that they are two very different things.

Two different matters, but both apply of course to people who come from other countries to join us here in Canada. Canada has always had an immigration policy, and I think we can be proud of the policy we have had during the last twenty or thirty years, and even up to now. Our immigration policy is generally one we can be proud of. However, the Minister will agree that sometimes implementation leaves something to be desired.

I have had incidents in my riding of abuses by the system. When the system abuses common sense all Members of
Immigration Act, 1976
Parliament go to see the Minister of State for Immigration knowing that he, in elected office, has the political sensitivity and sound judgment to correct some of the things that go wrong. Luckily, 1 have had many abuses corrected.
The Minister knows very well of the case of one particular woman in my riding. She came here on a visa with her husband and they bought a farm in my constituency. 1 only relate this case to give an example of how the system sometimes frustrates everyone and causes abuse.
That constituent of mine was a battered wife. She saw advertisements on television and decided that the appropriate thing to do after being beaten repeatedly was to report her husband to the police, which she did. Her husband was thrown in jail, and rightfully so. However, the immigration authorities then decided that since they both came here on the same visa if one of the two had committed a crime, which in this case was the one beating up the other, they both had to leave the country. The message to this woman was that if her husband beats her up she should not complain because she would be thrown out. That is in fact what the system said.
Luckily I was able to contact the Minister and he was compassionate enough to say that it would not work that way. The woman and her children, who were both born in Canada, were allowed to stay while the husband was thrown out. I have no difficulty with his being thrown out in the circumstances.
That is one example of an abuse. If I had another three or four minutes I could relate a number of others to describe the frustration with the system which may cause people to try to enter the country by other means. The honest and right way of doing it sometimes does not work.
I thank you for your patience, Mr. Speaker.

Thank you. Mr. Speaker, I strongly advise Hon. Members to reject Bill C-55. The Bill must be amended to prevent phony refugees from entering Canada, while ensuring that genuine refugees will always be welcome in this country.

Mr. Speaker, during the last few days of debate on immigration legislation, on both Bills C-84 and C-55, I have heard a multitude of complaints from the Opposition. Yet if there is anyone who should be concerned and should complain, and should commend the Government and the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) for his humanitarian instincts, it is one of my constituents, Mr. Fred Nachbauer of Nelson, British Columbia. He reads press articles from across the nation, and it appeared to him that Canada had allowed Sikhs to hit the shores of Nova Scotia and come in as legitimate refugees, which they are not.
Mr. Nachbauer was born in Germany and came to Canada with his parents at 11 months of age. Prior to 1976, he had to

August 18, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
reach the age of 14 in order to make a decision as to what citizenship he wanted, be it Canadian or German. By virtue of his parents' wishes he moved to the United States for a time. Over a period of years, both in Canada and the United States, he shared, with six brothers and sisters, a unity of family with wonderful parents. When that family returned to Canada, Fred decided to remain in the United States while continuing his education to seek his university degree.
The story becomes much more complex after that. Ultimately, Fred Nachbauer returned to Canada and his case fell between the cracks with the narrow interpretation of the Immigration Appeal Board that he should be deported to Germany. Tie did not speak German and had only been to Germany for one year since the time he was 11 months old.
I have spent time with Fred, his brothers and sisters, and his wonderful parents. I have also spent time with the Minister. I must tell the Flouse and Canadians that the Minister demonstrated the kind of compassion and understanding which, unfortunately, by virtue of whatever the circumstances, was not demonstrated by the Immigration Appeal Board at the time. I cannot condemn the Immigration Appeal Board, for it went by the book, but it failed to examine the parameters.
At this time I want to thank the Minister for all his endeavours on behalf of my constituent, and indeed on behalf of all Canadians.
Let me move to another matter that disturbs me deeply. I watched Rabbi Plaut on Canada AM last week. Canada was condemned for its handling of the recent pseudo refugees who landed in Nova Scotia. It was condemned for Bill C-84 and Bill C-55.
It is ironic that these pious words should flow from a man who selectively condemns Canada while choosing to ignore the record of Israel and the Palestinian refugees.
What is the immigration policy of Israel in terms of the Palestinian refugees? He chooses to ignore that babies who are kidnapped or bought on the black market or otherwise from their mothers in Peru or Brazil are allowed into Israel unencumbered. It may well be argued that those babies will be provided with a better life, but clearly they have jumped the legitimate process.
Rabbi Plaut, by his words, condemned all Members of Parliament, regardless of Party, who have taken the time and effort to write to Jewish prisoners of conscious in the Soviet Union. Parliamentarians of all stripes have followed that process for many years. They have written letters to prisoners and letters to the Soviet Government. It is a frustrating experience to all of us, but it is a joy when one wins a case, as I have experienced.
I suggest that when Rabbi Plaut speaks out against the efforts of the majority of parliamentarians in this House, he condemns us for our humanitarian actions. What about humanitarian actions? He condemns the outstanding humanitarian record of this Government and its Secretary of State for
External Affairs (Mr. Clark), who is a humanitarian of the first order.
He condemns Canadians for turning back the Jewish refugee ship, the St. Louis, from our shores in 1939. I was 12 years old when the St. Louis was turned back. There are very few Members who were much older than that. Most of the Members in this House were not even born when the St. Louis reached the shores of Canada, yet we are condemned for the actions of parliamentarians and the Government in 1939.
While I have not had the opportunity to examine the reasons for that action, whatever the reason may be, I find those actions to be most regrettable. I am sure that Canadians have apologized for it time and time again. Why must Rabbi Plaut raise it in the context of the current debate?
This Party, this Government, has a record of human rights unequalled by any other Party or any other Government. During the John Diefenbaker Government, Douglas Jung of Vancouver was the first Chinese Canadian to sit in the House. Lincoln Alexander was the first black elected to the House. He became Minister of Labour in the Clark Government and is now an outstanding public servant and Lieutenant Governor for the Province of Ontario. He was appointed by a Conservative Government under our Prime Minister. We led the world in our humanitarian effort to aid Ethiopians.
Let us compare Bill C-55 with the current legislation. According to the old system, there are seven separate stages in the refugee determination process, which takes up to five years. Bill C-55 provides four separate stages which hopefully will take no more than 12 months. 1 am astounded by the hyprocrisy that has been demonstrated by the Opposition.
The position of the Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) with respect to Bill C-55 and C-84 was best depicted in an editorial cartoon which needed no words. For those watching this debate on television, the cartoon depicted the Right Hon. Leader of the Liberal Party like this, pointing in both directions. Nothing else needed to be said because it spoke volumes for the position taken by that man and his Party.
Let us examine the position taken by the New Democratic Party. It is worthy to point out that the Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) said: "I do not see any need to recall Parliament this summer at considerable expense". At a time when Canadians are outraged, that is the educated response of the Hon. Member. The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) said: "I do not think it is really worth while, but of course that is up to the Speaker". Then, of course, we have the sage advice of the Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) who said: "If we continue to get on our shores individuals who suddenly come up and say, 'Look, we are refugees, take us in', I think we will probably have no choice but to seek a middle ground, and the middle ground that I am talking about is something like a holding centre or a detainment centre, what is commonly known as a refugee camp". I cannot but conclude-
August 18, 1987

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I am sure the Hon. Member would not wish to suggest that the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. March;) is a member of the New Democratic Party. Those comments were not made by a member of our Party.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco) has the floor.

For the record, Mr. Speaker, I skipped from the NDP to the Liberal Party without the Member being aware of that transition. However, if he feels more comfortable about it, I will identify the Hon. Member for York West as a Member of the Liberal Party.
In conclusion, I would like to quote the Leader of the Liberal Party. Upon the arrival of the boat off the shores of Nova Scotia, he said: "That boat might well have been apprehended and could have been turned back because this is not a legitimate refugee process". Enough said.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to make a few comments on Bill C-55 and indicate my opposition to the principles involved in this Bill.
1 believe all Members of our Party, as well as other parties, acknowledge that we have a very serious problem. There is a need to clean up the refugee determination process. However, we want to make it very clear that we do not feel this Bill addresses that problem in a serious and fair-minded way, one that is suitable for Canada in 1987.
I want to try to address the concerns of Canadians, particularly the concerns of my constituents who know that something terrible wrong has happened to the whole refugee determination process. Feeling that something has gone wrong, they tend to support Government legislation which claims to correct the situation. I want to try to show why this legislation cannot be supported by fair-minded people.
Let us begin by trying to establish a few facts on which I hope all Members can agree. First, over the last few years, Canada has had a fairly enlightened and progressive refugee policy. This was recognized by the world community last year when the United Nations presented the Nansen Medal to the Canadian people. Second, we can all recognize that the global refugee problem is becoming more serious. It has changed since the Second World War when the refugee problem was mostly centred in Europe. We received refugees from war-torn Europe. Later we received a great many from behind the Iron Curtain. For the last few years the centres of refugees have moved to the Third World and we received a great many refugees in the late 1970s from Southeast Asia. Today Central America is producing a great many refugees. It is at that point that we are starting to close the door.
The situation in Africa is one that staggers the imagination. There we have not only the typical convention refugee, the
Immigration Act, 1976
person who is fleeing from some kind of persecution, but we also have ecological and economic refugees.
It is estimated that in our world today there are between 13 million and 15 million refugees. Indeed, it has been said that over the last 30 years, 700 refugees per day have been created by the turmoil in our world. When 174 of these refugees land on our shores, we suddenly declare a national emergency and Parliament has to brought back into session.
The third fact which I believe can be objectively agreed upon is that western countries have become more restrictive in their refugee determination policy. Denmark, which had one of the most open policies, has now tended to close the door. The United States has recently passed very restrictive legislation. This legislation is intended to clamp down on illegal immigrants, many of whom are refugees, and it puts very severe penalties upon anyone who harbours those refugees or gives them employment.
The American refugee determination process has been rather slanted. One can get some idea of this from the fact that in 1982, out of 12,000 Salvadorans who applied for refugee status in the United States, only 26 were granted that status. This is obviously a very slanted process in the United States. So western countries have become more restrictive in their refugee policies.
Canada, because of an outmoded refugee determination policy, has become subject to abuse. We have seen a great many phoney refugee claimants. We have seen scams such as that of the would-be immigrants from Portugal, members of the Jehovah's Witnesses, who claimed they were being persecuted for their faith, a claim which was denied not only by the Government of Portugal but also by the Jehovah's Witnesses themselves.
Such an obviously untrue claim is nevertheless, processed through our rather cumbersome machinery and it takes up to five years, as many Hon. Members have pointed out, before the final determination is made. Because it takes so long, these phoney refugees have by then put down some roots in the community and are sometimes able to make a claim on compassionate grounds that they should be allowed to stay.
It takes up to five years before the end of the process for bogus refugees. That, of course, has to be cleaned up. As this dodge has become successful for some, it encourages still more phoney refugees to try the same kind of tactic. The result is that Canada has become known as a soft touch for phoney refugees. This kind of abuse increases resentment in Canada towards all refugee claimants. They are seen as queue-jumpers who are avoiding the normal immigration route.
In fact, refugees should be seen as quite distinct from people who are involved in the normal immigration process because it is quite a different situation.
This in turn focuses attention upon some of the more visible minorities who apply for refugee determination and it encourages a form of racism. It is important to eliminate this kind of

August 18, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
abuse. Although the abuse might be widespread and practised by people from many different countries, it tends to focus on one or two highly visible groups. This kind of focusing appeals to the latent racism or xenophobia which, I suppose, is found in all people and certainly Canadians are not immune.
We can see this if we look at the situation from the perspective of our history. In 1947 Mackenzie King indicated that there were not going to be any changes in our very selective and discriminatory immigration policy. He said he did not want to see anything which would result in "a fundamental alteration in the character of our population".
In the past we have had a lot of tension between Protestants and Catholics in this country. I can remember in the early 1950s when a moderator of the United Church, to which I belong, complained about our immigration process at that time because he said we were opening the doors to too many Catholics. He was not a particularly bigoted individual. He was a little bit behind his time and was playing on an old Protestant fear that Catholics were going to overrun the country.
The turning back of the St. Louis, to which a previous speaker referred, was based on the anti-Semitism which was then very prevalent in Canada and is still found just beneath the surface in the lives of many Canadians.
Governments have sometimes played on this kind of racism. The Winnipeg general strike of 1919 was led largely by British trade unionists or people who were descendant from British stock. Yet, in an attempt to give the impression that the Winnipeg general strike was of Bolshevik origin, a few people with Slavic names were arrested and deported. That kind of playing on xenophobia is unacceptable and we do not want to see it in 1987.
The 1976 Immigration Act specifically recognized the refugee category. In 1987 there is confusion in our thinking and in our feeling about refugees and how they relate to the whole immigration process.
First, there is a concern about the question of fairness. There is a legitimate objection to queue-jumping, if that is what is happening. When people abuse the process that has to be stopped.
Second, there is a fear of being overwhelmed by refugees. I pointed out that there are about 15 million refugees throughout the world. Last week the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister suggested that there are five billion people all wanting to come to Canada. That was rather irresponsible of him.
Third, there is the fear of many Canadians that our traditional values will be swamped by an influx of people from different cultures. Different peoples with different cultures do bring different values, but do we have so little confidence in our own values, so little belief in the things that are important
to us that we feel they will not be able to stand up in a multicultural society.?
Fourth, there is a concern about jobs. At some levels this is a valid concern. Certainly in times of high unemployment, if there is a great influx of unskilled workers, then it can depress wages at the bottom end of the scale. For that reason there has been a decrease in the whole immigration rate over the last few years. But in the long run we recognize that an increase in immigration results in a larger market, a larger consumer market. We bring in entrepreneurs, which is good for the economy in the long run.
What has been the reaction to this on the part of the Government? When the Plaut Report was brought in the Government ignored it, except to ask the standing committee to make recommendations on it. But when the standing committee brought in its report it was also ignored by the Government.
Finally, last spring the Government announced an administrative crackdown and then later on in the spring it tabled this legislation. It was not brought forward for debate until the last couple of weeks in June. Now the Government declares that there is an emergency. We have had a crisis building for years.
Bill C-55 does not address this problem in an acceptable way because it does not give the benefit of due process to the claimants. It allows the deportation of them to a so-called safe third country. But there is no such thing as a safe third country. No country is entirely safe for all people.
The Bill does not allow the possibility of refugee claimants to have lawyers representing them at an early stage. It allows for the elimination of up to 80 per cent of the refugee claimants before they ever reach the determination process. For this reason we oppose Bill C-55.
We urge the Government to bring in a process that is more in line with the recommendations made by Rabbi Gunther Plaut or by the Government's own Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration.

Mr. Speaker, for the past several weeks I have listened with some interest to the observations of members of the Opposition on the subject of refugees. 1 have heard them make some very curious statements. 1 propose to examine some of these statements during my remarks in the next few minutes.
Yesterday the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) representing the NDP, and a little later the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) representing the Liberal Party, spoke at length on the merits of refugees and the contributions they have made to the development of our country. They made these remarks as though someone were denying these facts, an inference totally unfounded and certainly not a view offered from anyone on this side of the House these past several days.
August 18, 1987

However, it was their choice of words in voicing their views yesterday which particularly interested me. Their observations, echoed by other members of both their Parties, clearly indicated that our prime concern as parliamentarians must be to help, to give comfort and refuge to those who reach our shores seeking asylum. This we are bound to do by UN agreement and by common decency and charity. This is our paramount duty and responsibility according to those Members opposite.
Indeed, we should be listening to the representations of Canadians, we were advised. This was said yesterday and in the days preceding. I beg to differ with this interpretation. I am of the view that as a parliamentarian my first duty is to Canada and my second is to my own constituents. My task is relatively easy in this particular matter. My duty to Canada and my duty to my constituents are one and the same.
What is that duty in this instance? On this topic of refugees my duty is to ensure that we have in place a refugee policy, a refugee determination process that is clearly and readily understood, fair, humane and enforceable. That is our prime duty to Canada as parliamentarians.
It is clear to anyone even slightly familiar with the current refugee problem that our rules are not clearly and readily understood. Consequently, they are neither fair nor humane, and most certainly they are not enforceable.
In other circumstances, members of the Opposition have had much to say about perception. Rules and procedures must not only be fair and just but be seen to be fair and just. My constituents do not believe the current situation to be fair or just. They do not believe the current administration of the refugee process to be fair or just to Canada or to them individually as Canadians. They are outraged at the flagrant abuse of the current system. They expect-indeed they demand-that Parliament, namely, all of us here on both sides of the House, accept our responsibilities and revise the rules, clarify the process, stop the abuses, deal firmly and appropriately with those profiteers who have conspired to circumvent the rules, those who have traded in cargoes of human misery.
How do I know that this is what my constituents feel? It is as a result of the hundreds of telephone calls I have received, as well as the hundreds of letters, numerous office appointments and countless chance meetings.
We as a Government have presented legislation to deal with this issue. What have we had as a response from the Opposition? After all, we are at the second reading stage, the stage at which basic principles are being debated. We are not in committee. We are not at third reading stage, a stage at which we might be debating the recommendations of the committee. No, we are debating the basic principles. Others have covered very adequately these principles.
What is the contribution of members of the Opposition, to give the Bill a six-month hoist, to shelve the matter until next February so that it can compete for attention with the next
Immigration Act, 1976
Budget now produced annually every February? The production of a Budget every February is yet another positive constructive action introduced by the Government. But what the opposition Parties really mean with their six-month hoist is that we should have no immigration rules, no refugee barriers, a policy of, "you all come". I do not hold that view, and neither do my constituents.
Of course we need immigrants for the country to grow. It has been said many times in this debate that immigrants have in the past and will continue in the future to make a very substantial contribution to our country, to the growth and development of Canada. Of course we must accept our share of legitimate political refugees. We do require a meaningful process by which we can determine who is and who is not a legitimate political refugee. Opposition Members have clearly indicated an unwillingness to clarify or more closely define such a process.
Indeed, we are accused of having a desire to punish those who illegally aid or abet illegal refugees who arrive on our shores or at our borders. Those who encourage illegal activity deserve to be punished. Since when are immigration or refugee laws any different from the other laws of this land? Are the opposition Members now arguing that robbery is acceptable if a person has some charitable activity in mind for the proceeds? Hypocrisy is alive and well on the opposition benches.
Opposition Members pretend to be against queue-jumpers. When it comes time to deal meaningfully with the problem, they do not want to deal with the issue. They would rather listen to the immigration lawyers, special interest groups, and even foreigners with vested interest, instead of the millions of ordinary Canadians who want an orderly, fair, and enforceable set of regulations to protect the health and security of our society.
It is entirely legitimate that we should confine refugee applicants until their state of health is determined, and whether they are a security risk. Equally, we have a right to determine who they are, how they arrived, and from where they came. Apparently, the Opposition is not interested in such matters. They pretend to be concerned about queue-jumpers, about fraudulent refugee claimants, and then resist reasonable efforts on the part of the Government to develop a fair and sensible process. No, Mr. Speaker, their response is to banish the subject until some time in 1988. That clearly underscores their view of the priority of this matter. They might just as well state honestly and openly that they do not believe Canada should have any refugee determination rules. Actions speak louder than words. There is no doubt of the effect of their actions.
Canadians expect us to deal promptly with this issue. We on this side of the House intend to proceed. The proposals contained in Bill C-55 compare very favourably with the

August 18, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
regulations observed by our international friends and allies. Bill C-55 will serve us well, and it merits speedy adoption.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to follow the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Crofton). He is a Member of Parliament I have respected since he has come to this area. I have served with him on committees, and I have always felt that he is a fair-minded person. 1 looked forward to hearing the manner in which he would present a defence for this piece of legislation, and I will take into account his criticism of the points raised by members of the Opposition when dealing with this Bill.
No one is arguing with the concerns of the Hon. Member or his constituents for a fair determination system for refugees. There presently is a system which was built in a time when there was not the same type of pressure, but it did conform to our international obligations.
The first question 1 wish to pose to the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich and other Conservative Members, is why are they supporting a Bill that clearly contravenes our obligations under the United Nations Convention for Refugees?
Not so.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: That is in your opinion.

Mr. Speaker, it is so.
If 1 may quote from our Immigration Act it states:
-fulfil Canada's international legal obligations with respect to refugees and
to uphold its humanitarian tradition with respect to the displaced and the
persecuted-
Perhaps the Hon. Member is not aware of the fact that in February of this year the Government cancelled or eliminated a special refugee status that had been established for oppressed and persecuted people. Under group sponsorship that allowed Canada to take people like the Baha'is from Iran, Falashas Jews from the Sudan, and Jews from Argentina, people who were not fully within the definition of convention refugees. That clause was cancelled or eliminated. The opportunity for this country to reach out to specially persecuted groups around the world was eliminated.
Is that the type of policy that the Member feels his constituents want to support? Is that the type of policy he, as a fair-minded person, is endorsing? When a person in another country is denied access to schools for their children, denied access to employment, and threatened with jail, do we as a country want to condone that? Do we want to condone the type of persecution faced by the Baha'is in Iran?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Where does it say that in Bill C-55?

I am dealing with Bill C-55. Bill C-55 is an extension of what the Government did in February under its new regulations.
Let us deal with the fundamental issue, which I do not think Conservative Members of Parliament understand, that our obligations are based upon universal access.
The Members opposite are laughing, Mr. Speaker. To them refugees are a joke. It is a way of making political points, and it is not a serious matter. If they want to continue laughing, let me say to them that ultimately the record of this House will be the historical record that they will have to live with.
The basic international commitment that we made when we signed the protocol of 1969, and successively, is that we would grant universal access. That does not mean that everybody is accepted. It means that everybody has a right to make a claim. It is quite clear under the United Nations that we can then set up our own determination procedure. That principle was endorsed by the Commons committee, obviously by a majority of Conservative Members.
Now there is legislation which contradicts that principle. How? It is clear. There is a screening proposal which automatically excludes or pre-screens one class of people when they arrive on our shores before they have a chance to make their claim. That contravenes our agreements under the convention. It is quite clear that we are setting up two classes of people. I think that probably better than anybody the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) is aware of that fact. That is a clear contradiction of the principle of universal access.
In debate last week the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) was probably the only honest Conservative Member because he said that was correct. We do not believe in universal access. If that is the case, let us get it on the table and say that the Government no longer agrees with its international commitments. The Minister of National Health and Welfare said so, and he was wildly applauded by other members of his caucus. But no one, including the Ministers for immigration, has had the nerve or the courage to say that is what they agree with, that they are prepared to break that commitment. That is one of the things that is wrong with Bill C-55.
The Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich has been a student of international obligations. I recall when he was a member of the joint committee studying external affairs that he made very eloquent statements of our need to support international obligations. He is now supporting a Bill that will break those obligations.
Not so.

The Hon. Member is saying, "not so". I say to Members opposite that if they do not agree with universal access then they are breaking those obligations. Clearly that is part of what this Bill is about. There cannot be pre-screening.
Another example is the refoulement procedure, a commitment made by this country time after time under UN Convention. Under Article 31 of the convention it states that a refugee
August 18, 1987

claimant is not sent back to a country from which that refugee claims persecution. That is the so-called refoulement clause. This legislation states that a person can enter Canada, they have 72 hours or three days, and then before they are sent back regardless of whether or not they are safe where they are going. That is a total and complete contradiction of Article 31 of the convention. Once again I ask Members if they know what they are doing? Do they understand that they are transgressing signed commitments? I do not think that they know what they are doing.
An interesting story appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press about the comments of the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner). It was dealing with Bill C-84, but let me point out that there is a clause in Bill C-84 which says that transportation companies will be required to screen refugee claimants before they board aeroplanes and to take away their documents. Then we discovered that a senior Canadian immigration official, Mr. Kirk Bell, was a member of the executive committee of the United Nations High Commission for Refugees which, several months ago, passed a resolution condemning the practice now included in Bill C-84. When asked about it, the Minister of State for Immigration said, "Gee, I didn't know about that. Somehow no one told me. Gosh, if I had only known".
It is an interesting contradiction or dilemma that a senior immigration official sits on an international body which decides that to rely upon transportation companies to screen applicants contravenes the convention, and three months later the Government brings in totally contradictory legislation and the Minister says "I didn't know".
This means that either the officials are not telling him or that the Minister is not telling the truth or that in fact the whole thing, as we suspect, has been rushed, hurried, and brought in to appease that public opinion, about which people talk, even though it will clearly violate everything Canada has stood for and will violate our international obligations.
The point is that it was not necessary. It did not have to be done that way. There was already in place a perfectly good series of models and recommendations on how to clean up the refugee determination procedure. We have the chairman of the committee in the House today, the committee which made recommendations on how it should be done. They were supported by the so-called special interest groups; for example, the Central Committee of the Mennonite Church, the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, and the United Church of Canada. Those so-called interest groups help people who are trying to help refugees. The idea that somehow someone who is involved in helping refugees is part of the special interest group and should not be listened to is not acceptable. The very people who sometimes risk their own lives and resources to help refugees are being cast aside as having no involvement or interest in the Bill. There was a solution.
Immigration Act, 1976
Hon. Members opposite suggest that somehow the Bill will clean up a mess which was not there. The fact is that they will create a worse mess. They will be challenged before the Supreme Court in terms of contradicting Article VII of the Charter. The granting of oral hearings will create an unworkable mess at our borders. It will create a clear and disturbing reaction in the international community when they see Canada contravening its obligations. It will create a worse problem internationally because the fact of the matter is that we will be contributing to the problem, not solving it, with this piece of legislation. That is the real issue.
It is unworkable and unfair, and it will make the problem worse.

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to join in the debate today. I will get to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) a little later in my remarks. Suffice it to say he was immigration Minister for some time and is part of the problem, not the solution. That is well documented, but I will talk about it later.
We are debating Bill C-55, a Bill which will change the procedure of determining refugees who claim refugee status in our country.
I represent a riding of some 220,000 people. It has grown 24 per cent between 1981 and 1986. That tremendous growth is continuing today. I believe that my constituency is a fairly good cross-section of Canada today. It has a mix of immigrants from all parts of the world. There are those who have come here as refugees. There are those who have come through the other streams of immigration.
An NDP Member today talked about two streams. There are really four streams of immigration, which I do not think people in Canada really understand. One of those streams is the refugee stream, and it is a separate one. We also have the family reunification stream, which again is separate. We have the entrepreneurial stream from which we probably realize some 5,000 or 6,000 people per year. We have the independent class, those who apply and may have skills required in Canada and are accepted as immigrants. We have four different streams.
Let me refer to what has been going on. It was going on in the years when the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry was the Minister of Immigration. Because the system we had for hearing refugee applications was bureaucratic and time consuming, the average wait for a hearing was five years, sometimes extending to seven years. By the time their hearings came up, whether or not they were legitimate refugees, they had purchased homes, got married, and had a couple of Canadian children. Of course the first person who went to defend them at their hearings five years later was their employer who said, "Gee, don't send him back; he is one of the best employees I have". Also the local priest or minister would support them, or even the convenor of the local soccer league

August 18, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
who would say, "he is the best coach 1 ever had. He is a pillar in the community".
Nobody is questioning whether or not they were good immigrants or good new citizens of Canada. The point was that the system allowed people to come to our shores, whether or not they were legitimate refugees, and load up the system so heavily that by the time their hearings came up it was almost impossible to take a negative position toward an individual.
When the Conservative Government took power in 1984 there were 20,000 people waiting for hearings. Word spreads pretty quickly around the world these days. All of a sudden Canada's system looked like an easy way to get into the promised land.
During the years when my hon. friend from Winnipeg-Fort Garry was the Minister of Immigration he knew of these problems. His record as Minister of Immigration is not a sterling couple of years, driving a person with a record over the border to give him a ministerial permit to get them back in. His type of immigration policy is well documented.
Let us look at what has happened. Every year since 1980 immigration through the refugee system has increased and increased to the point that last year they were coming in at the rate of 1,200 per week and the system could not absorb them. The way the system was set up we could not absorb that many people.
Had we not taken action, the estimates are that 40,000 people would have come in that way this year. What we are finding out is that 85 per cent of them are not refugees as recognized by the United Nations. They may be economic refugees looking for a better future. I understand that. 1 understand perfectly why people try to come to Canada, why they want to get into our wonderful country.
1 should like to refer to what the people in my riding have said to me, as well as to the calls and letters I have received. They represent people from a broad cross-section-people from Asia, people from Europe, and those who are many generation Canadians. A big mixture and they say: "We are a generous people". I disagree with Rabbi Plaut. He does not think we are a tolerant people. He said that in Maclean's magazine. He thinks Canadian tolerance is overblown. 1 disagree with the Rabbi on that. We are a tolerant people. However, taking into account every person who wrote me and every person who called, the bottom line is "don't play us for suckers". The bottom line is, "If you want to come to Canada, if you want a better future, go through the proper routes".
Canada has accepted refugees year after year. I hear members of the Opposition say that we do not care about refugees. I would like to remind them that it was a Conservative Government under the leadership of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) and the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) that brought
refugees from Vietnam, the boat people, to Canada. There was an outpouring of feeling for those people. They were legitimate refugees and it was important that they come here to find a haven and that Canada play its part. As a matter of fact, Canada played a magnificent part in that emergency.
This legislation will not stop legitimate refugees from coming to Canada. Canadians are generous people. We brought in 20,000 refugees last year and we will bring in the same number this year, but they will be legitimate refugees.
What the people of my riding are telling me and what I feel most earnestly is that we cannot have people abuse our system to come to Canada. All those who are legitimate refugees and immigrants will suffer because Canadians are saying all of a sudden, "wait a minute," and a backlash against immigration is beginning. That is dangerous. We do not need and do not want that in this country. We need immigration to grow. Immigration creates employment, it does not take jobs away from anyone. I believe the estimate of the Department of Employment and Immigration is that for every immigrant that comes to Canada, a job and a half is created, so we need immigration but we want legitimate immigrants and we want a refugee system that will assure that legitimate refugees come to Canada and that Canada plays it part in the refugee system.
Bill C-84 is now in committee and we are debating Bill C-55 today. 1 might remind Hon. Members that we are debating an amendment posed by the Liberals to put this matter off for another six months. That is the motion that is on the floor, put by the critic for the Liberal Party. He made a great speech in the House the other day but never mentioned once that he had moved the amendment to put this off for six months. Canadians do not want that. We will vote against that six-month hoist. We want this Bill to get into committee. We will have hearings in committee. If there are flaws in the Bill, we will take a good look at them. We will make sure that we are doing the right thing, but to postpone this with a six-month hoist like the Liberals would like to do is hypocrisy and Canadians know it.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, after hearing the spouting of the last Hon. Member, one would think that there was a true emergency and that this was something the Government had just discovered this summer. As Hon. Members know, the Government sat back for three years and did absolutely nothing about the situation. Finally it introduced legislation in the House in May, brought it back for less than three-hour's-worth of debate in June and never brought it before the House of Commons again until just recently.
It is obvious that the Government did not make this issue a priority until it felt that there was some overwhelming public opinion on it as a result of the landings in Nova Scotia this summer. The Government has not shown a true commitment to reforming the immigration laws of Canada.
August 18, 1987

The Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration studied this matter and members of all three Parties worked hard to produce a Bill of which all Canadians would be proud, a Bill which would recognize that there are genuine refugees and that there are problems with the immigration system, while also recognizing that there are very frequent abuses of the refugee system. The House of Commons committee studied this issue and came forward with concrete proposals. The Government has done nothing to introduce those concrete proposals to the House so we could have legislation of which all Canadians could be proud. Now, as a result of the landings in Nova Scotia, the Government wants to move quickly.
The committee to study Bill C-84 met for the first time last night and for the second time this morning. We have heard Conservative members of that committee urging that this matter be dealt with in four days. We have heard Conservative Members urge in the House that Bill C-55, the legislation we are dealing with now, be dealt with quickly.
I believe it is important that we actually look at the legislation we are passing so that we may understand its implications and ensure that we are not railroaded by public opinion of the moment. We should make sure that we do not commit in 1987 the equivalent of turning back a boat full of Jewish refugees in 1939. We should make sure that we do not have a recurrence of the way we treated Japanese Canadians in that same era. I am afraid that some Hon. Members from the government side are trying to create that same kind of public hysteria. They are building on the fears of Canadians rather than trying to make them understand the true situation.
It is obvious to me that more and more Canadians are realizing that Bills C-55 and C-84 are wrong, are faulty and were drafted without any real understanding of their implications. Reading some of the more recent editorials, 1 would point out that as informed journalists have looked at this legislation, they have realized that these Bills are bad and are ruinous to Canada's reputation for being fair.
Let me quote from the Winnipeg Free Press of August 14, 1987:
One of the reasons why thousands of people try to sneak into Canada either illegally or by claiming to be refugees is that the legal routes are unreasonably difficult. Canada discourages immigration except by people with needed skills which Canadians workers lack or with large personal fortunes.
A strong back, an adventurous spirit and a willing heart now count for nothing in the immigration system, though these were the assets which got the ancestors of most Canadians into the country.
In that respect, like many MPs, I have heard that Canadians are upset with the present immigration system. They are saying that we must do something to these people who landed in Nova Scotia because their own relatives cannot get over. That perception does exist, and again Conservative Members, the Ministers and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) are trying to promote it. They are trying to say that these people who landed in Nova Scotia are taking the place of legitimate immigrants. That is not true.
Immigration Act, 1976
Whether the Liberals or the Conservatives are in power, the immigration system of Canada is horrendous. People who should have been allowed into Canada have not been allowed in, whether they be refugees or immigrants who tried to qualify under other parts of the law. We find abuses that are heartbreaking because they keep families apart. People who want to come over here to make an honest and sincere contribution to Canada are denied that opportunity. People who would benefit us by their culture and industry are denied access to Canada.
Regardless of who is the Minister of Employment and Immigration at a particular moment, when you appeal to the Minister he or she refuses to exercise the prerogative to make exceptions. Like many MPs, I have written to the various Ministers responsible trying to get them to recognize the peculiar situations in which people find themselves. 1 have asked them to intervene, only to be refused.
It is not simply a matter of refugees landing in Nova Scotia displacing immigrant family members who are not yet in Canada. The problem is that the Government has not come to grips with the immigration situation. It does not have a policy which is fair to people from Chile, the U.K. or other parts of this world.
In my own riding there is a bank manager who wants to bring his uncle to Canada, an uncle that raised him. We have written to three successive Ministers pointing out that this is not just an uncle, but a much closer relation. The bank manager is willing to support the uncle. Yet we cannot get the support. Another constituent has an aunt in Chile and cannot bring her over. We have tried to get the Minister to act and he will not.
There are many problems with our immigration system but that is not a reason for rushing this legislation through the House. Neither Bill C-84 nor C-55 will do anything to resolve the problems I have talked about. This legislation will not create a fairer system. The problems will still exist under this legislation and people should not try to sell it as a fairer system which will allow aunts, uncles or cousins to come to Canada.
I only have a minute or two left and it is very unlikely I will have a chance to address this Bill again. If I had the time, I would like to quote from the Free Press or The Gazette, The Edmonton Journal, The Vancouver Sun or the Calgary Herald, all of which have editorials that can be found in today's Quorum pointing out how wrong the Government is with this legislation.
There are other groups, including the Manitoba Mennonite Central Committee, who are concerned. That committee wrote a letter dated August 14 to all Members of Parliament expressing their deep concern with this legislation. They point out the history of Mennonites and the fact that they may not have been allowed into this country under this legislation. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), who is a

August 18, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
member of that group, should look at his own history and ask himself whether his ancestors would be allowed in this country if this legislation had been passed 50 or 60 years ago.
A lot of Canadians should look at the legislation and ask if it is fair, and whether it deals with the problem in a way of which we can be proud. 1 think the answer most fair-minded Canadians will give is, no, it is not fair, it is not something of which we can be proud, and it will not address the real problems we face. For that reason I suggest the Government withdraw the legislation. If it refuses to do so, certainly we should spend the required amount of time to make sure it gets thorough study.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the opportunity afforded me today to comment on Bill C-55.
A poster was distributed by the UN High Commission for Refugees showing a picture of graffiti on a refugee camp wall which says, "Refugee go home". The caption under the picture says, "He would if he could". In that message we have the essence of refugees and what distinguishes them from other immigrants.
Immigrants seek new horizons and opportunities for settlement. These are the people referred to when we talk about the influx in the early part of this century into Canada, and in the settlement and development of western Canada. Their desire to emigrate arises from their own ambitions and a desire to break out of an old routine. Their current environment is too limited. Perhaps in the case of Polish or Ukrainian immigrants it is the opportunity to own and develop land that brings them here. There is a chance to fulfil their dreams.
Refugees, on the other hand, are a people with a stake in their community. Sometimes they are among the leaders and the most progressive. They are persecuted and forced out of their own countries because of who and what they are. They may be members of minority groups like the Ugandan Asians Canada admitted in the early 1970s. They may suffer because of their religion, like the Iranian Baha'is. They may be political dissidents, members of a particular social class or people of a certain nationality. Canada's policy is that although refugees are not voluntary migrants, they can be helped to rebuild their lives by being given an opportunity to emigrate and settle in a country like Canada. That is what our policy was all about; providing durable refuge to refugees for whom no other remedy is available.
For that reason we have two programs. One is a program of assistance. Most of our assistance involves contributions to help refugees in camps in other countries who are, like the Afghans, waiting for a political settlement so they can be repatriated to their own country. It also involves bringing large numbers of refugees to Canada as immigrants through our immigration process or programs. Other speakers have noted the details and they have been repeated time and time again in this House. However, the Government will pay for the settlement of 12,000 refugees this year. Private groups and
individuals will bring in 6,000 or more for a total exceeding 18,000.
The second program deals with protection, for refugees who simply arrive, legally or illegally, and ask for a safe haven in Canada. When dealing with true refugees, this is the first priority and this is our obligation. We are some distance from most refugee producing situations, and we are not accustomed to this role. However, for the individual refugee who simply arrives, the provision of safe haven without qualification is vital to the process. That is what Bill C-55 is all about; swift, sure and generous response to those who do not have safe haven and who would be persecuted if they were forced to go back to their own countries. I want to repeat that; a swift, sure and generous response to those who do not have safe haven and who would be persecuted if they were returned to their own countries.
This role is not discharged by this Government by simply accepting everyone who claims to be a refugee. We do not discharge the obligation of the Government simply by accepting everyone who comes to our shore and says, "I claim refuge as a refugee".
The dilemma that we face is to find a fair and effective way to separate those who need our protection from those who do not. That is really the bottom line. Our experience in Canada and that of every other major receiving country in the northern hemisphere shows that in an open refugee system the clear majority of people who claim refugee status are not refugees at all. Among real refugees many are simply changing one form of prior protection for another at the expense of those who have no protection whatsoever.
We know that people have been arriving at various points across Canada and ripping up their passports and travel documents because they had in fact already received refugee status in another country such as Germany or Holland. This must be stopped.
The principles behind Bill C-55 are, first, absolute guarantee of protection for those genuine refugees who do not have safe haven or did not have an opportunity to acquire it elsewhere. The principle of the Bill is not to allow a refugee who has refugee status in another country to come to Canada's shores and rip up their travel documents and any indication of the status they do have, and then apply for and receive that same status in Canada.
Second, we want the highest standards of procedural fairness including the benefit of the doubt to the claimant demonstrated by certain features, the first being oral proceedings. Every person arriving claiming refugee status is allowed to tell their story at a proceeding in their own language expressed in their own way. They will do this in front of two-member panels, two people will be entrusted with listening to the story and making a decision. If there is a split decision, the benefit of the doubt would go to the claimant. The proceedings
August 18, 1987

will be non-adversarial. In other words, there will not be a prosecutor attempting to trip up or in any way badger the individual making a claim for refugee status. The next point is that everyone will have a right to counsel.
This is a simple and flexible procedure to ensure speedy identification of genuine refugees and early removal of abusers. We must have that to maintain the integrity of the refugee system in Canada. We must have legislative protections for those determined to be refugees, including the right to apply for permanent residence. If we accept people as refugees, they must be legislatively protected to allow them to apply for permanent residence.
Bill C-55 constitutes a fair compromise and respects the ideals toward which well-intentioned people and countries direct themselves. This system as a whole has more safeguards and offers higher standards of procedural fairness than others in effect and is one which all Canadians may be confident will not expose anyone to the risk of persecution.

Mr. Alfonso Gagliano (Saint-Leonard

Anjou):	Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate this morning on Bill C-55.
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I want to say that before the House was recalled last week, all Members had a chance to meet with constituents in their respective ridings and had many opportunities to discuss the refugee question. Mr. Speaker, this is an international problem and, as you know, there are many countries that receive far more refugees than we do. Nevertheless, Canadians are upset about the methods used by some groups to enter Canada.
Since 1980, under the Liberal Government, there was an awareness that we might have this kind of problem and a number of studies were ordered. Toward the end of the Liberal Government's last term, the studies and recommendations were before Cabinet, and after the election, when the Conservative Government took over, it had access to the same recommendations, and at the time it could have acted on those recommendations and found solutions to the problems we are facing today.
But no! The Conservative Government decided in the fall of 1984 that it would ignore recommendations that were the result of studies that had taken several years to complete. They ordered other studies, which, as we know, reached the same conclusions.
The fact that three years later we are confronted with a crisis of this magnitude is the fault of the Conservative Government's inaction, a Government which today is trying to take advantage of popular sentiment to pass a Bill that will prevent genuine refugees frorp entering Canada.
Mr. Speaker, there is a lot here that is just a matter of semantics, but we all agree we must not let phony refugees enter Canada. However, we do not agree with the methods for
Immigration Act, 1976
dealing with this problem. We on this side of the House believe that Bill C-55 does not provide a solution. The problem is with the process. The Conservative Members tell us that Bill C-55 will provide for a screening process to determine whether refugees are genuine or not and to do so more quickly. However, after examining the Bill, we find that the process has become more complicated and will take more time.
Second, when drafting this legislation, and I am referring to Bill C-55 and Bill C-84 as well as any other immigration policy the Government may wish to table, did the Government ever wonder why we have so many phony refugees in our country? One Hon. Member said 85 per cent of our refugees were phony refugees. Is there any particular reason for this?
Mr. Speaker, I can tell you about my experience in the riding of Saint-Leonard-Anjou where there are a number of communities other than the Francophone or Anglophone groups. My constituents are upset, just like anyone else, when they hear about cases where people who have a brother or a sister, a cousin or other close relatives, are prepared to give their homes and their money as security to get their relatives to Canada. So they are prepared to offer every conceivable guarantee and even regular employment, yet under the terms of the existing immigration statute these people simply cannot be allowed into Canada. We are understandably indignant when we see other people coming in through the back door. In this respect we agree that something has to be done.
If the Government were to look at it this way, Mr. Speaker, I think it would promote the kind of immigration policy which at least would give hope to people who are anxious to resettle in Canada after complying with all legal requirements.
But right now, Mr. Speaker, for all practical purposes Canada's doors are shut tight. But there is a way for somebody to enter Canada: he lands here with a tourist visa, hires a lawyer, claims to be a refugee and, owing to the lengthy process involved, he is allowed to remain in this country.
After three years in office and fully cognizant with studies made and reports submitted before the last election, the Government still has no policy. People who made their move before this Government was elected did not take that problem into account. If today we had an immigration policy fully consistent with the turn of events since the beginning of this country, people who are willing to work and earn an honest living would be allowed in to resettle here and promote prosperity in this beautiful country, Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I am proud to take the floor in this House today. I am one of those who benefitted from the Canadian policy under which it was possible to come here and entertain every hope of success. As it happens, Mr. Speaker, I must wonder whether I would even have been able to gain entry into Canada in the 1950s if I had been faced with today's immigration laws and such measures as Bill C-55 and Bill C-84. Mr. Speaker, that is where all Hon. Members should ask themselves the question. I am pleased to see that we have here with us in the House the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
August 18, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
Weiner). 1 am sure he is quite close to the ethnic communities in the Montreal area.
Instead of adopting stringent legislation to create the impression everywhere in the world that Canada is closing its doors completely or putting people in jail who, for humanitarian reasons, help legitimate refugees enter Canada, we should develop a comprehensive immigration policy. That is why Canadians generally are furious. We need a comprehensive immigration policy to give hope to all those who want to come to Canada. For the relatives who are here, we need a family reunification policy, Mr. Speaker.
Therefore, I hope that Bill C-55 will be redrafted in its entirety. Instead of closing our doors, we should open them to all those who want to immigrate to Canada, while sending them at the same time clear and precise messages that when they come here they will have to respect. . . While in the process of integration, they will have nevertheless to take into account the Canadian context, accept Canadian tolerance, respect our laws and build a future for themselves and their children.
Mr. Speaker, you are signalling that I still have a few minutes left. That is a debate which would definitely require more than ten minutes to truly examine all the aspects of this Bill and develop a real immigration policy. 1 hope that my colleagues, especially those who belong to the Government majority and can determine the fate of the Bill, once this debate is over, will announce an immigration policy that will give hope to those who want to come to Canada and become full-fledged citizens.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to participate in this debate because of the importance of the issue and the widespread public concern. 1 have been impressed, as have other Members, by the intensity of interest on the part of the public on this issue and by the hundreds of telephone calls to my constituency office, as have been received at the offices of many other Members.
I want to bring into this debate some representation of the opinions expressed by citizens to me, because it is their opinions that provide us with the strongest argument against the entirely unwarranted amendment which the Liberal Opposition has put to the motion on Bill C-55.
Let me cite these sentences from letters that have come to me from across the country. The first is from Halifax. "Surely Canada has to be master of its own destiny". Another letter from Quebec states, "I heartily approve of your proposed tough new legislation to deal with the so-called refugees". One letter from Scarborough states, "What kind of message are we sending to the rest of the world?" Another states, "These people knew what they were doing when they paid their money to someone to illegally bring them to Canada". Another letter states, "It is extremely unfortunate that in our complacency
the silent majority will once again be the losers". Here is a letter from a Toronto person who says, "Why should these people be allowed to jump the line?" Again, from Toronto, "One has only to set foot in Canada and the patsy Canadians will spend years and millions of dollars fighting each other over whether you can remain". Again, "They have entered Canada illegally". A letter from London, Ontario states, "A clear signal must be given to the world that Canada is no dumping ground for impatient, dishonest, unreasonable people". A resident of Willowdale states, "It has been proved beyond any doubt that it is really profitable to be a violator of the law than to be law-abiding". Also from Toronto, "Protest against the cynical outlawlessness as exercised by another boatload". Another letter states, "We are incensed at the slackness of this Government". Another states, "It is likely that before this letter comes out in print the politicians who want only more votes might have caved in". A resident of Niagara Falls, Ontario states, "When are we going to stop being the immigration patsies of the world". Another letter from Saskatchewan states, "Obviously a quick one is being attempted and we cannot help but feel somewhat frustrated that this modern-day rum-running operation would have even a chance of success". A letter from Wynyard, Saskatchewan states, "1 don't care if these people had come from Iceland, Ireland or the U.S.A., what they did was wrong". subsubtopic: CHOICE OF MONTREAL AS SITE FOR NEW SPACE AGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the third time this year, I rise in this House to ask the Conservative Government for an answer as to the location of the future space agency. The city of Montreal is getting impatient and wants to have that agency in its area.
The Canadian Space Agency will have a central and determinant role in the development of Canada's space industry. Its economic impact, especially on employment, will be very significant. I therefore believe it is essential that its location be announced as soon as possible. That decision has been postponed for too long. The Canadian aerospace industry is for the most part concentrated in Montreal. It is in Montreal that Canada's aerospace industry had its beginning some 25 years ago. Today, Montreal remains the capital of that industry in Canada.
Although a number of cities and provinces would like to host the Canadian Space Agency, they all recognize Montreal's importance and experience in that field. It is therefore time that this Government also recognized this and located the space agency in Montreal. Foot dragging has been going on far too long. The Government must take action and select Montreal as the capital of the Canadian aerospace industry.
