subtopic: SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH TAX CREDIT-COST TO TAXPAYERS
SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH TAX CREDIT-COST TO TAXPAYERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) has now confirmed by letter that the Scientific Research Tax Credit is going to cost Canadians over $1 billion and has given figures that indicate that cost may go to $2 billion or the equivalent of $76 for every man, woman and child in the country. That is equal to almost half of what Canada spends annually on research and development.
This boondoggle was created by the Liberal Government, but when the Conservative Government had a chance to slay the monster it gave it new life by a grandfather clause which allowed alleged abusers to continue to take advantage of a rich tax boondoggle.
Despite assurances from the Minister that his Department would give all the necessary resources for tracking down fraudulent projects, the track record is not good. Not only have there been only four prosecutions after years of investigation but the Department has not collected one additional cent since March, 1986. A government official has now admitted that the Government is no longer going to go after many of the culprits. It is thereby giving up millions and millions of dollars which belong to Canadian taxpayers.
When is the Government going to live up to its responsibility to the Canadian people? When is the Conservative Government going to admit its responsibility and take action against abusers who have milked the ordinary taxpayers of billions and billions of their hard-earned dollars?

Mr. Speaker, I have here the Quarterly Economic Review published yesterday by the Department of Finance. The highlights are found on page 1.

August 18, 1987
Real growth picked up very strongly to 6,3 per cent. The final domestic demand was also very robust, growing at 6.1 per cent.
Residential investment continued to be the strongest component of final domestic demand as housing starts rose to levels not seen since 1978. Business non-residential investment spending surged.
The trade balance improved in the first quarter. Exports of goods and the terms of trade both increased. Employment growth increased to a 4.2 per cent annual pace. The unemployment rate dropped to 8.9 per cent in June, its lowest level since February, 1982.
These, Sir, are tremendous accomplishments. 1 am proud to be a supporter of a Government which has turned the national economy completely around in such a short space of time.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MILITARY COLLEGE STUDENT OFFICERS
TRIBUTE TO MILITARY COLLEGE STUDENT OFFICERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to get on the floor of this House a subject usually has to be about wars, rumours of wars, disasters and neardisasters, crises, real and imagined. I would like to say a word about something positive, encouraging and even heartwarming, something that I was impressed by during a brief
visit to the College Militaire Royal de Saint Jean, Quebec, where I saw face to face 218 young Canadians selected from many hundreds more for training as future officers in the Canadian Armed Forces. They are now undergoing an intensive program that takes them each day, seven days a week, from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m., from parade square drilling to lectures on all dimensions of military service.
They are impressive for, at the age of 18 and 19, they are mature in their acceptance of discipline, their readiness to meet a challenge and to serve a cause greater than themselves. 1 refer to them because they and others at other defence colleges of Canada are an inspiring demonstration of the quality of Canadian young people.
The next time I sing the national anthem and sing: "O Canada, we stand on guard for thee" 1 will want to keep in mind these young people prepared to spend the rest of their lives doing just that.

Mr. Speaker, today marks another sad chapter in the inadequate regulation of financial institutions by Governments with the sell-off of some of the Principal Group's assets. This will not significantly help the 67,000 persons who hold uninsured contracts with Principal subsidiaries such as Associated Investors and First Investors. Had the federal Government simply insisted that all RRSP contributions be covered by deposit insurance, many of these small investors could have been secured.
Since the federal Government gives significant tax savings to RRSP contributions, it is clearly in the Government's interest to see that these contributions are as safe as possible. Instead, about $115 million of the losses by Principal's subsidiaries are lost RRSP contributions.
How much longer will it be before the small investor, who puts trust in the Government which encouraged Canadians to invest in RRSPs, gets better consumer protection? Many investors in Alberta and in other parts of Canada want that question answered today. They want the Government and Parliament to enact legislation which will enable the CDIC to give Canadians the protection to which they are entitled.

subtopic: HIGHLAND PIPING AND DRUMMING-CANADIAN BANDS TAKE FIRST AND SECOND PLACES
HIGHLAND PIPING AND DRUMMING-CANADIAN BANDS TAKE FIRST AND SECOND PLACES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the last remnants of Canada's colonial past disappeared short days ago in Scotland when two Canadian pipe bands came out on top in the world championship for Highland piping and drumming. This is the first time that Canadian bands have superseded Scottish bands in this way. The 78th Fraser Highlanders, and Simon Fraser University Pipes and Drums, placed first and second respectively. They are to be commended for their excellence, and for representing Canada so well in their endeavours.
In recent years leading Canadian pipe bands have distinguished themselves by the freshness, the creativity, and the finesse which they have brought to traditional piping and drumming. The fact that this is now recognized, accepted, and even acclaimed in Scotland itself is something in which all Canadians should take pride. Canadians too are now able to say with confidence: "Here's tae us, wha's like us. Damn few, and they're a' deid!"

SALE OF WEST KOOTENAY POWER AND LIGHT TO UNITED STATES CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fight to keep West Kootenay Power and Light under Canadian control continues today in British Columbia where the Kootenay-Okanagan Electric Consumers Association is attempting to appeal the decision of the B.C. Utilities Commission to approve the sale to the U.S. based UtiliCorp.
The provincial and federal Governments have made a bad error in judgement in approving this first ever sale of a public utility to a foreign-owned company. The U.S. Government recognizes the perils of foreign ownership of its utilities, and it has banned similar actions.
The only reason the Minister responsible could give for the approval was that market forces determined the outcome, and that Canada would, in some way as yet unspecified, benefit from foreign ownership of this utility. It is a sad day when the federal Government abandons Canadian ownership of public utilities.
I urge the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) to stand up and prevent the foreign takeover of our public utilities. Canadians would prefer to retain ownership of our public utilities.
Frank Lauer of the B.C. Fruit Growers' Association put it well when he said: "When you own the cow, you sell the milk; when you sell the cow, you buy the milk".

subtopic: MANITOBA-EFFECT OF PROVINCIAL SURTAX ON INCOMES
MANITOBA-EFFECT OF PROVINCIAL SURTAX ON INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we just heard some good news from the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), but I am sorry to have to bring forth some bad news.	-
Since July of this year working Manitobans have been taking home less pay thanks to the NDP provincial surtax of 2 per cent on their incomes. Most Manitobans have no choice and must still live in Manitoba and pay such excessive taxes. Others in Manitoba have options.
The Royal Bank is now in the process of relocating some of its administration from Winnipeg to Alberta. Why? The last Manitoba budget increased the capital tax on banks from 1.9 per cent to 3 per cent, costing the Royal Bank $4.5 million more. Payroll tax was increased by 50 per cent to 2.25 per cent. These anti-business taxes are driving an increasing number of employers, employees, and investments elsewhere.
The excessive taxation of the New Democratic Party in Manitoba is causing businesses to relocate. When businesses relocate, so do the jobs. It is only fortunate that these businesses and their employees can still find provinces within Canada where taxation is progressive and business is welcome.
Honestly, Mr. Speaker, with these kinds of penalties can we really blame new businesses and investors for staying away from Manitoba?

Mr. Speaker, the recently announced western diversification initiative is good news, not only for my home province of Saskatchewan but for all western Canada.
This initiative, under the leadership of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight), will assist entrepreneurs to develop new ideas into projects which will create not only jobs but will help to diversify the western Canadian economy and make us a little less vulnerable to the uncertainties of the world commodity market.
The injection of this new money, $1.2 billion, is proof positive that we have put our money where our mouth is. It represents a solid commitment on the part of the Government to assist regional development of western Canada.

speechtext: Order, please.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I believe that because of the Hon. Member's performance today, instead of having a full House, we have a royal flush as can be seen by looking at the House.

Mr. Speaker, I will not try to top that comment. This is getting a little too risque for my tastes.
1 would like to address the legislation before the House because it is a very serious piece of legislation and it has very serious implications for Canadians and Canada's international reputation.
1 want to tell you how 1 size up the situation we are facing today. We are here in an emergency sitting of the House in the middle of the summer to deal with a Draconian piece of legislation concerning refugees. Why? Basically because of the concern of Canadians over the fact that the refugee process is not working and the Government said this is our opportunity to recover our standing in the polls. This is our opportunity to take on the Liberals and NDP and come out on the winning side of public opinion. The Government has for so long been at the bottom of the opinion polls and out of favour with the public that it saw this as its opportunity. That is why the House was called back this summer. That is why we have this legislation before us.
We should remind ourselves of what the Government said before it came into office and how it acted after it was elected in order to evaluate what it is saying in this debate. When the Conservatives ran for office, they started out by condemning the Liberal Party and the Liberal Prime Minister, now Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner), for abuse of the patronage system. The now Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) criticized the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition in debate and won public approval. Yet what did he do once he got into office? Exactly the same thing the Liberals did. He took the same kind of immoral and depraved actions regarding the patronage system that the Liberals did. He carried on with the same kind of activity he had condemned. That is the difference

August 18, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
between the promises and the actions of the Conservative Government.
We have a parallel in this situation. The Government is promising to fix the refugee determination process. Most Canadians have come to the conclusion that the process is not working. It is being used and abused by people who simply want to come to this country without going through the normal process. That is what so many Canadians find unfair. We all recognize that the process needs to be changed, that we need an adequate and just determination process. So the Government called the House back and brought forward its legislation.
Does the legislation do what it purports to do? It is clear that it does not. One thing it does do is to give the Government the opportunity to say it is coming down hard on the abusers. Of course it is, but in the process it is also tearing apart the democratic traditions of this country. We have heard from human rights advocates across this country. We have heard from representatives of the churches. We have heard Rabbi Plaut who did a thorough study of the refugee determination process. We heard the UN say that this legislation is going to put at risk the possibility of genuine refugees coming to this country. Therefore the legislation is not doing what it purports to do, that is, eliminate the abusers while at the same time allowing for a fair and efficient determination process by which genuine refugees can come to Canada.
In fact it breaks with a generous Canadian tradition of providing a sanctuary for those whose lives are threatened elsewhere. It threatens those who are struggling against the dictatorship in Chile and who are threatened with torture and death. It tears apart the Canadian tradition of sanctuary in the name of fixing a system that is not working.
Not only that, if passed by the House in its present form, which I doubt will happen, it will be torn apart in the courts. The effort will be wasted because it does not do what it claims it will do. It should be withdrawn and humane, effective legislation, which allows for the elimination of abusers while at the same time maintaining our compassionate and open approach to people who need sanctuary, introduced.
We call upon the Government to wake up and stop trying to rush this legislation through. It should realize we are not going to let this go through quickly because we want to make sure the process takes into account not only the abusers of the system but also the human rights of those who need sanctuary.

Mr. Speaker, if you and I were to examine the mail I have received from one coast to the other, along with telephone messages in my constituency office, and I am sure it is comparable to that received by other Members, we would see that there are certain common features to the expressions of opinion which have arisen without stimulation from those on Parliament Hill. One of those features is that there has been no racism expressed by the people of Canada in their opposition to the
ingress of what they see to be illegal immigrants to this country. Over and over again I have had it said to me that the concern of the population is not based on any consideration of race at all.
None at all?

None at all. The Canadian people cannot be accused of racism no matter what the Opposition, including the Hon. Member, may wish to suggest. The people of Canada are saying to us that, regardless of the race of the person concerned, he or she will receive equal treatment before the law and not special privilege.
The second feature is that they want fairness for all, including those who have been waiting patiently, not without frustration, for years in their attempts to gain legal acceptance in this country. The people of this country see what seems to be manifest unfairness in the possibility of someone gaining entry to this country by what appears to them to be a trick. They are asking Parliament and the Government of Canada to provide legislation which will make that kind of fairness possible.
Next, I find a concern among Canadian people for the rule of law. We are a law-abiding people. We are a people that have historically been characterized by a commitment to order as expressed by the laws of the country. It seems to people an utter affront to that tradition of law, that respect for order, that people at will, be it a large group or one or two or three, can somehow insinuate themselves into this country in a way clearly contrary to the demands of the law and the requirements of regulations. They are, therefore, asking us to provide the Government with the authority required to re-establish the rule of law in terms of refugees.
Further, I believe that the Bill before us should be supported, not only by the government Party but by every Member of the House, because there is clearly a demand from the people for action. They have been frustrated over an extended period of time as they have seen the laws broken, traditions flaunted, and unfairness apparently rewarded. We are told that they want some action. We are trying to hurry the Bill through the House but the Liberal Opposition wants to give it an extended examination, a six-month hoist.
We are faced with the utter dismay of the people of Canada at the prospect that once again they may be thwarted. They are appealing to us, and this Bill is an answer to that appeal, an attempt to give them action in the face of need. We have been called together to make a decision.
Along with that demand for action I take it from the mail and calls that I have received that there is an extraordinary but nonetheless impressive message from the people that they wonder if anybody is really in charge. They are demanding to know whether anyone is really in control of admission into the country. If you can just show up on a beach or at an airport
August 18. 1987

and somehow, without qualifications or credentials, find yourself in the country with de facto admission for one, two, three or perhaps five years, they wonder whether the Government really is in control.
1 take that question very seriously. If the Government and the legislature of a country are not really in charge, in what sense are we a country? If we do not have control over our own borders, what kind of country are we? That is the situation to which we have come in recent times and which we are attempting to correct, and not with any lack of justice or compassion for those who legitimately merit the term and designation "refugee".
I am sure that all other Members, like myself, have read the Convention of 1951. It is clear from that document, to which this country has been a signatory and to which the Government, like others before it, is committed, that a refugee has designated, covenanted rights. The ambiguity arises over who is a refugee and who determines that. It is quite clear that the country itself determines that refugee status in accordance with the terms of the covenant and its historic application.
1 submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the Bill before us is in accordance with that and will stand the test of challenge. We have every right, indeed every duty as a Parliament, to put our imprimatur upon it and to make it the law of the land so that the Government, elected by the people, given a mandate to govern, will truly in this instance be in charge.
I am not unaware that this Bill, like any other that has been introduced in this House since 1867, might well be improved by this amendment or that. I think it would be approaching hypocrisy if either side of the House were allowed to suggest that there is nothing that could not be clarified, nothing that could not be refined. However, in debate on second reading we are talking about the principle of the Bill, the clear message, and of that there can be no doubt if we take the people of Canada seriously.
I am aware that the opposition Parties do not take the people of Canada seriously, that they are really elitist Parties that are with the people if the people are with them and their secret knowledge of the truth. I am appealing to them through you, Mr. Speaker, to listen to the ordinary Canadians, of whom they are apparently so fond, and take seriously what the ordinary Canadians are saying, namely, "give us some action, give us the rule of law, put the Government in charge again".
I have been impressed that the Liberal Opposition, for one, has opposed this Bill. It tried to give it a six-month hoist. 1 was impressed as well that less than a month ago the Liberals were saying that the Government was at fault because it had not turned the boat back. Now the Liberal Opposition wants to turn this legislation back. 1 ask them to be consistent, to be concerned, not about turning the boat back but about turning the clock ahead to today, to putting this nation in tune with the times, and to giving us legislation which can cope with this problem which is of this day and age.
Immigration Act, 1976
The legislation and rules of the past are no longer adequate. To be fair to those who drafted them, they may have met the need then, but they do not meet it now. We have need for legislation which takes seriously an entirely unprecedented development. We have 12 million refugees in various centres in the world. We have frightening population pressures in various parts of the world. There are 5 billion people sharing this globe, many of them crowded into small conurbations-16 million, 18 million, or 20 million in a massed urban sprawl. We can appreciate that there will be great pressure for many years to come on persons to find new opportunities and to offer themselves as refugees when, according to the convention, they do not meet those criteria.
We have a need for this legislation. The Government was right to call this House back through the Speaker to deal with an emergency situation in an emergency way. I hope that we will see reason and pass the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about Bill C-55 and to support my party which considers that the bill provides no solution to the tragic situation and to the international problem raised by the determination of refugee status.
Instead of being consistent with the tradition of assistance to refugees Canada can be proud of, the provisions of Bill C-55 put a stop to any progressive initiative in that area. The proposed legislation does not allow for an accessible and quick mechanism for determination of the refugee status nor does it give sufficient protection through a hearing before a qualified board and through a fair appeal procedure.
The Liberal Party is opposed to Bill C-55 because it essentially provides for a new process for the determination of refugee status without taking into account the Plaut report and all suggestions made by organizations dealing with refugees.
If the Conservative Government is serious and honest about consulting those organizations regarding the reform of the refugee determination process, it should not try to pass legislation in which the basic principles of the future process are laid down.
Besides, this view is largely shared by immigration lawyers and many humanitarian agencies. There are, among others, the concertation group for refugees, SOS Refugees, the Civil Liberties Union, the Societe quebecoise de solidarity international, the Immigration Lawyers Association, YAssociation des juristes quebecois, the Inter-Church Committee for Refugees, the Standing Conference of Canadian Organization Concern for Refugees, Amnisty International and the Island Refugees Society of British Columbia.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party is not opposing Bill C-55 for the sake of filibustering. This is not a partisan issue but a matter of pure common sense. For instance, if you look at the pre-screening process, it builds up a wall all around the system that we claim to improve. The pre-

August 18, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
screening process is very discretionary and it prevents the full accessibility to the process.
As well, if you look at the Refugee Board, its proceedings are supposed to be non-accusatory, but it is the Crown Prosecutor who will put forward all the relevant facts. There will be an adversarial situation with an officer working for the Department. Where will he find those facts? From the prescreening process? Why do we put together refugees and immigrants?
Of course, if you look at the appeal mechanism, that is the appeal with the agreement of the Federal Court, if the Court is unable to learn new facts, to re-evaluate the credibility of the claimant or to ask for the opinion of the NGO, it has no real power to review the procedure followed or the relevant facts. We believe that the quality of the system as a whole depends on that of the appeal mechanism. In addition, while the claimant asks for the right to appeal, he will be deported. This procedure is quite inhumane and could be unconstitutional under Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that Canadians have been misinformed. Racist feelings are on the rise in Canada, and such a Bill will exacerbate the situation instead of educating Canadians.
1 believe that this is also the opinion of many Canadians. It is time to review the refugee determination process and to initiate an extensive information campaign on refugees. The great majority of Canadians do not know the difference between a refugee and an immigrant.
In the case of immigrants, the receiving country is entitled to set criteria and to accept only those who meet them. It is quite different for refugees. Canada has international obligations. Under the Geneva Convention, the refugee claimant is entitled to assistance. It is not a privilege. Most Canadians and many Members of Parliament are not aware of this. Many forget the political difficulties faced by many people in their own countries.
When you think about apartheid in South Africa, the military dictatorships and police repressions in many Latin-American countries, religious intolerance in Iran, the foreign invasion in Afghanistan, and so on, you are more willing to welcome those who fear persecution in their own countries and seek refuge in Canada.
As emphasized by Rabbi Plaut, compared with the magnitude of the global refugee problem, the task of recognizing the status of those who claim refugee status here, in Canada, is relatively small.
The information campaign which should be initiated should emphasize the economic contribution of newcomers as well as differentiate between immigrants and refugees. We have to put an end to the myth that foreigners are taking away jobs from Canadians.
Many economic studies dealing with immigration have shown that it is impossible to establish a cause-effect relationship between the number of foreigners admitted in this country and the economic situation. A number of economists maintain, however, that by increasing the number of potential consumers in a market, immigrants contribute positively to the economy. In short, it is our whole approach towards immigration which must be improved by increasing this openmindedness and generosity which have characterized Canadian men and women for so long.
This enlightenment of attitude which is urgent should go hand in hand with the reform of the refugee determination process. I feel that its implementation should offer the perfect opportunity to set in motion a refugee awareness campaign from coast to coast. This bandaid solution which the Conservative Government is suggesting today with Bill C-55 seems to be both useless and harmful. If it were adopted, I believe that the government, unfortunately, would delay reforming the refugee status determination process, contrary to what a great many groups involved with refugees are seeking.
In this Bill, Mr. Speaker, we cannot find any recommendation put forward by the special committee created to deal with Bill C-55. Although several groups appeared before the committee, unfortunately, we have the impression that the committee never existed. I wonder why the Government creates such committees. Is it simply for window-dressing purposes, when we realize that not a single recommendation made by this three-party committee which submitted a unanimous report appears in this Bill? I will say, therefore, that 1 have great reservations about Bill C-55 and will certainly vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, today I believe this country is facing problems at many different levels which will not be solved by legislation such as Bill C-55. Our concern is and certainly should be about the increasing international problem of refugees. We have a responsibility to have some input into an international solution and to seeing that the oppressive Governments that are ignoring human rights face international disciplinary action so that people will be able to stay in their own countries where they want to be, safe and secure.
I believe all Canadians are proud of our country which has been built from the different ethnic backgrounds of people who have come here in various ways, including the refugee and immigration process. 1 believe we have also been careful to ensure that people remain in contact with their own cultures so that they do not deny their roots. This has enriched the fabric of Canada and certainly made us stronger.
The kind of legislation before us does not help to maintain the international image we have had over the years. While 1 did not think this would be the first Bill to which 1 would be
August 18, 1987

speaking in the House of Commons, I felt it was important that 1 share with Members of the House the experience I had when we called for our community to adopt and sponsor 4,000 refugees in 1979. While the Government of the day had a quota of 8,000, we challenged communities across the country to sponsor these refugees. There was an overwhelming response in the country and within a month the quota was changed to 50,000.
1 believe all Canadians were very proud of the Indo-Chinese who came here, and 1 think the Government of the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and his Minister of Immigration, the present Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald), certainly deserve credit for their action.
It is a tragic and sad day for our country to be faced with the legislation in front of us now. It partly results from the generous action that was taken in 1979 because the number of refugees coming to Canada began to increase. Of course, the cumbersome method of defining a refugee was in place, a very cumbersome method which has not been able to respond to the need. I do not believe there is any disagreement across the country nor in this House, from what 1 have heard, about queue jumping. No one wants anyone to jump the queue. Certainly those people who arrive on our shores legally are not queue jumping. The real problem is that the present Government has cut back on family reunification by 10 per cent. Therefore, people who have applied and have been waiting for many years in the proper way, through the proper channels, are feeling bitter and angry because the numbers have been cut back.
I am disappointed when I hear some Hon. Members refer to things they heard from their constituents which do not always encompass the most altruistic kind of feelings. I can be a witness to some of the letters and phone calls I received when we put forth Project 4000. They were not always very complimentary. Some things that were said were less than what we would want to hear from people. However, I think we countered that reaction by showing that there was the other part of Canadian society who opened their arms and hearts, showing their generosity and proving we have a better country today because those 50,000 refugees came to Canada.
I feel that what has motivated many of us strongly is that we realize we are not proud of our fathers and mothers who allowed the kind of legislation to happen-and a lot of it was not legislation but regulation-that said many Jewish people had to go back and be murdered because we would not open our hearts and arms to them.
In examining this Bill we can recognize that it is just as cumbersome. We are not allowing people who are declaring themselves as refugees to have even full access to counsel. Because of this there will be people who will have to go back to
Immigration Act, 1976
the country which will persecute them before we ever realize it what we have done.
I am sure some of that rationale was expressed in these very Chambers in 1939. 1 hope we will not be part of encouraging that kind of thing to happen again. Certainly reports that have come from non-governmental organizations, from the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration and from Rabbi Plaut have all recommended things which I believe Canadians can live with and be proud of. What is really being said in those reports is that we want to have a fair and efficient system. We want to have a system where people can be heard, where they can be seen to have universal accessibility.
I was quite shocked to hear yesterday that people did not understand what universal accessibility was. All we are talking about is that it does not matter what colour one's skin is or what part of the planet one comes from, we are all part of the human family and should have the right to be heard. That is all we are saying. At the moment there are about 20,000 refugees in this country who have been here for four or five years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: More.

Yes, and probably more, because the process, has been so cumbersome. Because of this cumbersome process what we are going to do is to punish people who are running for their lives.
I come from a riding which has some very strongly committed volunteers who work day and night to help save the lives of some people from Central America. It seems to me that as these volunteers help to get these people into Canada, not only will they be seen to be criminals but certainly the people whose lives they are attempting to save will not be saved. I think that is something that is very serious. I do not think it is something that anyone in this country wants to have happen.
Surely the Government will recognize, through all the presentations made to it individually and through committee, that there is an easier way to accomplish what it wants to accomplish. I think today, the day we are speaking on this legislation, is the day to say to the Government that there is another way. We agree with the goals it is trying to attain but it is doing it in a very punitive way. Surely to goodness we are talking about a global village where we all live as part of the human family. We are saying that within that human family there are ways of dealing with each other's problems without causing chaos. Without causing chaos we can save each other's lives if we have legislation that is efficient.
I would heartily recommend to the Government that it withdraw this Bill. I believe we should begin to have a parallel system, one which deals with refugee determination efficiently and quickly as well as one which deals with immigration separately.
Right now the Canadian public is very confused about the chaos the system is in. I do not blame them for reacting the

August 18, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
way they are. However, I think the responsibility of this House is to ensure that we have a system that works, a system that is efficient, generous and fair, in the way most Canadians want their system to work.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard that Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, let me begin my remarks on Bill C-55 by recalling once more the chain of events which led to the recall of the Parliament of Canada from recess. Going back to August of 1986, Members will recall the arrival of 150 so-called Tamil refugees off the coast of Newfoundland. When that event happened, most Canadians were prepared to give the benefit of the doubt to the new arrivals and in that connection they were allowed to come into and remain in Canada. But what surprised a great many Canadians was the process by which these people entered Canada.
They were shocked in many cases to recognize and to understand, and to be told, that there was no real way these people, the so-called Tamils, could be prevented from coming into Canada or could be not allowed to stay here. This quite understandably led to a review of the refugee provisions. I think it is fair to say that that led the Government to construct the legislative provisions now contained in Bill C-55. It was introduced in the House of Commons in May, 1987. Some people say that it took too long a time, but who can judge the process? Sometimes legislation takes months, sometimes it takes years. The fact is that there was a Bill introduced in the House of Commons in May of 1987. It was debated and brought before the Members of the House of Commons on June 18, 1987. The representative of the Liberal Party, the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), introduced an amendment at that time which would give the Bill a six-months hoist which would put it into oblivion. That amendment was supported by the New Democratic Party. We just voted on and defeated that amendment a few moments ago in the House of Commons. That is why we are here. It is because the opposition Parties did not want Bill C-55 processed.
That is what we are talking about in relation to refugees. We are talking about legal process. We are not talking about the status of individuals. We are not talking about the fear and pestilence that pervades many countries in the world. We are not talking about people escaping from persecution. We are talking about the legal process. This Parliament of Canada, this House of Commons, is responsible for the legal process in this country. However, what has happened is that we as Members of Parliament have abdicated that responsibility by moving amendments like the six-months hoist for legislative measures such as Bill C-55 instead of coming up with constructive legislation to deal with what is the real problem in the process.
That brings me to July 12, 1987 when there arrived on the coast of Nova Scotia 174 East Indians who entered Canada illegally and said: "We are refugees", and our system collapses because our system does not handle that situation. Why does it not handle that situation? Because once one is in Canada claiming to be a refugee then the legal process no longer works.
It was said that we were faced with our obligations under the UN Convention respecting refugees. I think Canadians were shocked and outraged to learn that under that UN Convention a person in Canada claiming to be a refugee is entitled, for example, to access to the courts and to legal counsel in connection with that access. They are even entitled to public relief. Article 23 of the convention states that the contracting state shall accord to refugees lawfully staying in their territory the same treatment with respect to public relief and assistance as is accorded to its nationals. Not only do we have to accept refugees under certain circumstances, we have
August 18, 1987

to open the public coffers and pay them money, provide them with assistance and legal aid.
We all consent to that. That has been the position of the Government of Canada. We uphold the accord. But surely we must have the right to determine who comes into Canada and who is a refugee. Surely such a process has to be put in place so that we will not be faced with people who decide that they are coming to Canada, that they are going to claim to be refugees, that they are going to take advantage within our nation, our territory and our home shores, of the UN Convention, whether or not they are escaping from fear of prosecution or difficulties in another country, whether or not they are prepared to tell us what has gone on in their past history that would entitle them to special refugee status in Canada. That is why Canadians are outraged. They want to know what is happening. They want to be in a position to render a judgment. When that judgment is rendered, and rendered effectively and properly, I am sure all Canadians will support it.
I am sure that all Canadians will welcome refugees into the country. 1 am certain that all Canadians will afford such persons every item listed in the UN Convention, every guarantee of freedom and of liberty. That is what we all want. But we want to provide that sort of assistance only after a proper legal process has been observed.
Anybody-Liberal, Conservative or New Democrat-who denies the outrage of the public in this situation is simply not facing the true facts. 1 have heard members of the Opposition stand in the House and accuse the Government of fanning public outrage in this case. That is nonsense-absolute nonsense. One wonders how they can hope to represent the people of Hamilton Mountain or any other constituency across the country if they are going to make accusations like that against the Canadian people who were genuinely outraged by this event.
What we are doing is responding to that concern after trying to calm the people after trying to say: "Listen, we can take some time to resolve this problem". That was not the mood of the Canadian people. They wanted parliamentarians back at their seats working on this problem. That was the only course of action that could be sensibly taken, which is the course of action that was taken. Anyone who does not want to sit in the House of Commons to try to resolve this problem here and now has no right, in my opinion, to be here in the first place. The people told us what they wanted to do and we are trying to react to it.
My friend, the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse), said it very well. He said that we are not here to write laws in stone. This is not Moses coming down from the mountain with the tablets. We are here to write laws of practical application to deal with real problems. We are here to cure the mischief that exists in our society and to try to do something about it. If we make a mistake, then we can correct it. We do not have to wait years or centuries. We do not have to wait for anybody else to tell us what to do; we can recognize
Immigration Act, 1976
our own errors. So we are looking at Bill C-55. It is an attempt to cure what is an obvious mischief in our system, that is, the lack of process in dealing with persons entering Canada and claiming to be refugees so that they can get the benefit of the UN Convention which we readily observe.
Bill C-84 has already been referred to committee. It is a Bill which is intended to rid us of the mischief of those people who would help people invade Canada under improper circumstances and profit by it. We now have to deal with Bill C-55 which will give us an opportunity to deal effectively, speedily and fairly with people who arrive at our doors.
People from Upper Canada often annoy us in the maritime provinces and the Atlantic coast. They sometimes think that we are a little backward. I want to point out to those people from Upper Canada that it is not easy to get an ocean-going vessel into a small place such as Pubnico Bay, a beach on the coast of Nova Scotia. It is more or less like flying an airliner into Malton Airport without consulting air traffic control and over-shooting it and landing in some small airport in some county town.
In order to get an ocean-going vessel to the coast of Nova Scotia at a point such as that one has to avoid all the normal sea routes and all the navigational aids and benefits as well as the Port of Yarmouth and the Port of Halifax. That is exactly what was done. So I say this to Hon. Members from Upper Canada. Do not be surprised when people from Nova Scotia say: "What the heck is going on here? We know that those people who arrived on that vessel were avoiding the lawful process by which people enter Canada. We know that they did not disclose their identity to the traffic controllers. We know that they strained to put the ship in that particular place. So it is no wonder that we are suspicious of those who are involved in this process, no matter what difficulties they faced at home".
How can we get rid of that suspicion? We can only get rid of it if there is a fair hearing at which the facts are disclosed. And what facts were disclosed? The facts that I heard disclosed were the tearing up of identity documents, allegations that did not fit the facts about where the group had come from, how they had arrived here and how they got off the ship and so on. By the way, it was never made clear whether there were 174 or a great many more aboard.
I am well aware that bad cases make bad law. I think that is something that we want to avoid. But I marvel at my colleagues in the Opposition who talk in general terms about refugees and who talk in general terms about immigrants and who do not want to come to grips with the mischief that exists in Canada, that is, people seeking to enter Canada illegally.
We talk about fairness in our system. In 1986, the following immigrants entered Canada. There were 7,000 from the United States; 6,800 from India; 6,400 from Vietnam; 5,800 from Hong Kong; 5,100 from Poland; 4,900 from Great Britain; 4,400 from from Jamaica; 4,100 from Philippines; 3,600 from Guyana; and 3,000 from El Salvador. Does that

August 18, 1987
Immigration Act, / 976
sound like racial prejudice? Does that sound as though we were trying to exclude people from some areas and not admit people from others? That sounds like a pretty fair distribution of 50,000 people to me. Yet what does The Vancouver Sun state? It states: "PM's recall has taste of racism". 1 want to tell the editors of The Vancouver Sun that there is no racism involved in this issue. There is fairness to all Canadians involved, as well as fairness to refugees and, in particular, fairness to the immigrants who are already in Canada.
1 have people in the Punjab right now who want to come to Canada through the legitimate process. 1 have a heck of a time with the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) trying to get permission for a visitor's visa for these people. So do not tell me about racial prejudice. We want to talk about fairness, not prejudice. We want fairness. We want fairness for the people in the Punjab who want to come to Canada now. What we all fear will happen out of this is that if we do not achieve a proper process, if we do not achieve a fairness, then there will be a backlash against all immigrants. People will say: "If you cannot establish a decent process, a fair process, to bring refugees and others into the country, then do not bring anybody in. Keep them all out".
If we scratch the surface we often find, unfortunately, that there exists discrimination. But our job as parliamentarians is to ensure that we have a fair system, that we have a good system, that we have a system that will be observed by all people so that there will not be any discrimination. It is the system that prevents discrimination. The people cannot be changed but they can be made to observe a system. That is what we are trying to do with Bill C-55. I believe we are well on the way to having a fair system with this Bill, but we need some help and support from all Members of Parliament and all members of the public.

Mr. Speaker, the last intervention by the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) as well as the earlier intervention by the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse) were a mix of rhetoric and good intention, as well as confused notions about what is the real intent, thrust and purpose of this Bill.
It was disappointing that the Chairman of the Human Rights Committee, the Hon. Member for Scarborough West, would develop a speech the way he did without bringing forward in his capacity the importance of ensuring protection for asylum seekers, legitimate asylum seekers, who are, I am sure, one of the main preoccupations of the committee which the Hon. Member chairs.
The Members opposite are aware of the preoccupations that stem and flow from this Bill. They know that there are serious flaws in this measure. There are flaws in the pre-screening system and the process itself, the safe third country concept, the refugee board, the appeal system, and other aspects. This
measure has been put together without taking into account the important principle to which Canada has adhered for decades and which has been recognized by the United Nations, that is, that asylum seekers who are in need of protection must be protected and given an opportunity to apply.
Perhaps this may sound partisan coming from a member of the Official Opposition. I wonder if the Hon. Members for Scarborough West and Halifax West realize that one of their colleagues, the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais), who is the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, himself expressed some serious criticism of this very measure in this House as recently as five days ago. He stated it in the following terms:
-the Government intends to tighten the admission of refugees via Bill C-55, which will guarantee that the process remain arbitrary, confusing, and endless.
He further stated that the changes in the refugee determination envisaged and proposed by Bill C-55 are such that it would be practically impossible for a great number of legitimate refugees-note the word "legitimate"-to apply for refugee status. This was not said by a member of the Opposition, but by a member of the Government, one who is knowledgeable about this matter because of his role as the Chairman of the committee that studies matters related to immigration.
The same Member also commented that other rational and appropriate solutions to this problem exist, solutions that would not break an international agreement on refugees and could not be challenged in court on the basis of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Note the words that this measure in Bill C-55 contains sections that could be challenged in the courts. Unless it is modified, this measure could end up in the courts. This would tie up the Government in lengthy hearings because of badly drafted and poorly thought out legislation.
The Hon. Member for La Prairie also stated:
The best way to put the smugglers out of business is to dry up the demand for their services. The best way to stop the queue jumping is to shorten the queue. In short, if we want more orderly borders, we need more liberal borders.
It was courageous of the Hon. Member for La Prairie to issue a press release on this matter in which he commented on Bill C-55 and described it as follows:
It proposes a series of changes to the refugee determination process which would make it almost impossible for many genuine refugees to make a claim, and is in probable violation of both the UN Convention on Refugees (which we have signed and ratified) as well as our own Charter of Rights and Freedoms-
That sums it up, Mr. Speaker. That will explain why we on the opposition side put forward an amendment to hoist the measure entirely, in order to convince the Government that a clean alternative had to be introduced. That would not have been necessary if the Government had indicated that it would be willing to make certain basic changes of the type pointed out by the Hon. Member for La Prairie. Unfortunately, that did not happen.
August 18, 1987

It strikes me as curious in this debate that an element of urgency was created last week by the Government on the necessity of moving the Bill through the system as quickly as possible. In one month, it will be three years since the Government came to power. In 1984 and 1985, the Government also had the benefit of studies on the question of refugees and also of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration which produced a substantial amount of information and advice upon which to draft a Bill that would meet the needs of the situation. Yet the Government took until May of this year to introduce this Bill. The Bill then sat on the Order Paper after first reading. There was no sign of urgency and no panic, everything seemed to be calm. On June 17 the Bill was brought forward for debate for three hours, and that was the end of that Bill. It was not seen again.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: What did the Liberals do?

Because it was so badly flawed, and because the Liberals put forward such good counter-advice on how to improve it, the Government withdrew and did not know what to do. Instead of having the honesty and saying, "There are some areas where changes can be made, give it second reading and we will get it through", and also instead of listening to the advice of its own members of caucus-the Hon. Member for La Prairie is a very reliable source-why did the Government not listen to the advice by the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration? Why did it take almost three years to come forward with this piece of legislation?
Finally, we are facing this notion that we must move very quickly. The Government could have saved itself days of debate. It could have saved itself these exchanges, which I hope eventually will make some impact. On this side of the House we have repeatedly brought to the attention of the Government the flaws of this Bill and the importance of this Bill being written in such a manner that it will not be challenged in our own courts because it infringes on the Charter. That business concerns everybody. It is a very important matter. It is also important that we ensure that Bill C-55 take into account the important principle that we want to make it possible for asylum seekers in need of protection to be able to apply in this country. It has been done in the past. We are willing to support the changes that are within these basic principles. We know that it can be done, and we insist that the Government introduce the essential amendments in order to make it a viable piece of legislation that can be supported by all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, when reflecting upon what has been occurring in the House over the last few days, there are many, including myself, who are puzzled by the events which have transpired over that period of time in view of the history of the matter that we are deliberating.
Immigration Act, 1976
It is perfectly clear that there has been a great deal of concern in the country that our refugee determination process was open to abuse and subjected to abuse. There have been a variety of reports on the issue going back three years. We have had the Plaut report, the Robinson report, and two reports of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, all of which addressed the issue within the context that the refugee determination process as it exists now has been dragged out for so long that that in itself invites abuse.
There has been within Canada not only a clear consensus that the problem exists, but a clear consensus about the cause of the problem and the solution. This has been going on for quite some time, and it went on without any action by the Government until late spring.
With a history of inaction, we are suddenly brought back to the House of Commons on an emergency basis to deal urgently with an issue, the solution to which was clear and has been clear to everybody for a long time. Therefore one would have thought that in a matter of this sort, involving as it does extremely important human and humanitarian issues, the House of Commons, this Parliament, with the co-operation of all sides could have been able to act on a consensus about the solution to the problem we are here to address.
This raises questions. In view of this consensus and the identification of the problem and the solution, what has been the behaviour upon getting back here? The Government introduced Bill C-55. It also introduced Bill C-84. If one looks at what has happened here and tries to measure what the Government and Members on the government side have been involved in, one has to be deeply suspicious about the fact that we were called back here in the middle of summer to address a matter which could have been addressed a long time ago. When one listens to the rhetoric, one is really inclined to identify something on the government side other than a pure determination to address the problem which all Canadians have identified.
We have heard screams and complaints of queue jumping. We have heard allegations of reverse racism. We have heard intimations that we who have questions about the particular legislation before us are accusing the Government of racism in questioning it.
Let me just give an example. The Hon. Member from a riding with an extremely long name, the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen)-
It is a nice name.

It is a beautiful name, but it is excessive in its verbiage. Just the other day we heard him say that the Leader of the New Democratic Party had reflected upon a previous incident involving Sikhs landing on Canadian shores, and the Hon. Member, having identified within that elements

August 18, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
of racism, documented by all historians since that time, was accusing the Government of racism because this Bill and Bill C-84 were somehow related in a racist way to the landing of the Sikhs in Nova Scotia.
Those of us who understand the battle against discrimination and the expression of racism understand that in the absence of specified and regularized procedures with clear guidelines and opportunities for appeal, all of which elements are absent from Bill C-55, a situation is created in which individuals have an opportunity to express personal views and attitudes that could be prevented by appropriate provisions in the legislation. That is in no way to be interpreted-and I would say it would require a deliberate interpretation to see it in any other context-in a malevolent way.
Let me make a plea. The Government has submitted Bill C-55 as its solution. It is contrary in significant elements-in respect of the screening process, in respect of the concept of a safe third country, in respect of the inadequacies of its appeals and in other respects it is deficient as compared with other propositions which have been advanced. We know that the Canadian Council of Churches, the Canadian Labour Congress, and the Canadian Civil Liberties Association-a whole host of organizations interested in the refugee determination process; respectable, thoughtful, concerned Canadians represented by a variety of organizations-see the Bill as defective in significant respects.
If one looks at the suggestion of the Canadian Council of Churches, which is identical in significant elements to the proposition advanced by the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, one sees that it makes it possible for everyone who would claim refugee status to have access to the determination process. It meets the requirement for appeal, eliminates the notion of a third safe country, and provides at the same time that the whole process will be over in a matter of months. Indeed, it can be argued that the Government's proposition would be more time consuming in its implementation.
My plea is a simple one. Let us recognize that there is a consensus within the House on the need for a rapid and fair determination process which will eliminate abuse. Let us set to work constructively in committee to consider amendments which will strengthen the legislation. Let us do this as parliamentarians, let us do this as Members of this noble House, and let us do this as Canadians concerned as much with abuse as we are with fairness and humanitarianism.
This should not be too much to ask. Commensurate with that proposition, I would seek from the Government an undertaking that it will not eliminate from its appointees to the legislative committee, if that be the case, those people who have not adhered to the rigid line of opportunism which the Government has struck. Bring back the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais). Bring back those others who have given careful consideration to the issue. Let them join with us in constructing legislation which will be universally accepted
by Canadians, which will meet the issue of abuse, which will ensure the fairness that the vast majority of those not given to excessive rhetoric would support.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to say a few words in respect of Bill C-55 which deals with amendments to the refugee determination process.
I appreciate the opportunity because I, like most Members of Parliament-and in fact I suspect that it would be all Members of Parliament-have spent this summer being deluged by telephone calls, by letters, and by personal visits from constituents in connection with the arrival on July 12 of some 173 men and one woman on the shores of Nova Scotia. The message I got, as I am sure all Members of Parliament did, was that my constituents felt that these arrivals were queue jumpers and gate-crashers. They felt that they had butted into the line-up. Canadians have all at one time or another experienced being in a line-up and having someone try to get in in front of them. By and large, we do not like that sort of thing. There was a feeling that these people were butting into the line and that in that sense, they were illegal immigrants.
Another message came to me as well and that was a message of concern for the security of Canada. 1 suppose that was underlined by the Senate special committee report on terrorism which was released, interestingly enough, during this period of time. That report said that our present refugee process constituted a gaping hole in the security of Canada. It was that sort of thing that caused another outcry from my constituents.
I found it very interesting to note which constituents that message came from. The first group it came from was a delegation of the families of the survivors of the Air India crash. They expressed to me concern about the possibility of a gaping hole in our security system caused by the refugee process.
The second group that expressed concern to me came to me just as Parliament was recalled and I was on my way back to the House of Commons. This group was composed of representatives of the Sicilian community. In my constituency, there are about 10,000 Canadians who came originally from the Pachino area of Sicily. They too conveyed the message to me that they did not want potential terrorists getting into Canada through a leaky refugee determination process.
The message came to me as well just today when I received, as I am sure did other Members of the House of Commons, a letter from the President of the Hindu Federation of Canada. He as well expressed that same concern about the gaping hole the refugee determination process leaves in our security system. The message has come to me and to other Members of Parliament from many, many sources. We have heard not only about the need to do something about queue jumpers and gate-
August 18, 1987

crashers but also about the need for plugging the security holes in the process.
By and large, the people who communicated with me said that we should ship those who arrived illegally back immediately and if we are not going to ship them all back immediately, we should detain them and then ship them back. However, I got the sense, not only from the people who called me and came to visit me, but from the people in my constituency that there was another message there. That message was that we are prepared to see genuine refugees enter Canada, no question about that, but we do not want people using the process in order to butt in and get ahead of people who have been following the rules and waiting for years to enter the country legally as immigrants.
In my view, the reason that people decided there was a group of people trying to enter the country illegally revolved around the fact that every morning and every evening when they turned on their radios or television sets or when they picked up their newspapers, they were getting reports of people who had waded ashore not at a regular port of entry but at a fishing town on the coast of Nova Scotia. They were getting reports about people who did not present their passports when they came but ripped them up on the beach. They were getting reports about people who asked news reporters where they could catch the next bus to Toronto or Montreal. They were getting reports that alleged that some of them were saying that if they were ordered to kill, they would kill.
The people were not getting the other side of the story from the press or the media. They were not being told of the true meaning of refugee status. They were not being told of the distinction between a refugee and an immigrant. They were not getting the message that we were bound by the Geneva Convention, which we had signed as far back as 1969, to accept legitimate refugees and not to turn them away. They were not getting the message that in 1985, the Supreme Court of Canada had decided that anyone who is physically present in this country, whether here legally or illegally, is entitled to all the protection of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Those rights and freedoms, of course, include the right not to be held improperly and without just cause, the right to bail, the right to counsel, and the right to a fair oral hearing. All of those things flow automatically to those who are in Canada, legally or illegally, claiming refugee status.
I found it to be most unfortunate that the media and the press were telling only one side of the story. I do not want to say that that was universal, but by and large that was so. It is understandable, then, that after hearing only one side of the story, Canadians would get up in arms. It is understandable, after hearing only one side of the story, that they would not give us much time to try to explain the other side of the story to them. Indeed, it is not an easy story to explain. It is complex and involves many different steps. When one has made up one's mind in advance because of stories read in the newspaper or seen on television, it is very difficult to accept the comments
Food and Drug Regulations
of a Member of Parliament or a constituency assistant who is trying to tell the other side of the story.
That, of course, led to the Government introducing Bill C-84 and to the debate we are having today on Bill C-55. This whole process is designed to speed up the refugee determination system, which has resulted in a backlog of something like 20,000 cases. In speeding up that process, the whole idea with which everyone agrees, whether in Opposition or Government, is to reduce the amount of time people who are not legitimate refugees are in the country and, by reducing that amount of time and sending them back when it is decided that they are not legitimate refugees, to discourage others from coming. The idea is to set up a system that is fair and equitable.
In order to set up such a system, the Government introduced in February of 1987 some control measures. Those control measures were introduced at a time when the flow of refugees was about 1,200 a week. Those control measures cut that flow down to about 500 a week, and this legislation has now tried to put in place something that will replace those temporary measures with a fair system with which Canadians will agree, a system that will allow legitimate refugees to enter the country but at the same time discourage queue jumpers from entering Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It being 5 o'clock, the House will now proceed to the consideration of Private Members' Business as listed on today's Order Paper.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FOOD AND DRUG REGULATIONS SUGGESTED DRUG CONTENT LABELLING
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FOOD AND DRUG REGULATIONS SUGGESTED DRUG CONTENT LABELLING
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Food and Drug Regulations in order to require the labelling of all drugs, irrespective of their intended use, in a manner that would include a quantitative list of all medicinal and non-medicinal ingredients.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my main purpose in presenting this motion to the House for debate is to gain the support of my colleagues, and alert them to the difficulties faced by many Canadians, young and old, who take prescription and nonprescription medication without knowing its complete contents. This is a very serious matter for a person with a known allergy to or low tolerance for a certain substance. In some cases people wish to avoid a substance because they know it causes them to suffer adverse reactions. In other cases, people have experienced an adverse or allergic reaction and a list of ingredients on the product label will establish which substance caused the reaction. That way the substance in question can be

August 18, 1987
Food and Drug Regulations
avoided in the future. By labelling all ingredients in drugs a person can determine which product contains the offensive substance and can avoid that product. I consider this to be basic information.
The arguments are probably similar in some ways to the debate which took place when the Government introduced a similar requirement for foods in 1976. Many of the arguments faced by the Government in opposition to that labelling apply to my motion as well. Some of the fears were that labelling would reveal a company's secret recipes to the competition. Consumers would not utilize the labels because they would not bother to read them or, if they did, they would not understand the terms. As well, it would be costly and difficult to list ingredients on food packages. None of that happened. In fact, the consumer has greatly benefited from the introduction of food labelling legislation.
In linking food labelling to my motion I wish to point out that the April 27 issue of Maclean's magazine featured a cover story entitled "Food That Can Kill". It is evident that many of the arguments put forward in the debate over food additives also apply to my motion. The article indicated that sometime in late 1964 breweries in Quebec began putting increased amounts of a chemical called cobalt sulphate into beer. It had been used for several years to make the foam on a glass of beer last longer. However, during the next six months 48 beer drinkers in Quebec became ill and 20 died. It was the most dramatic episode in Canada so far in what has become a worldwide debate over the safety of chemical additives. We do not want anyone to have to die before making mandatory the labelling of all ingredients in drugs.
The article went on to say that individually additives may be okay, but taken together with other chemical or nutritive factors they may cause adverse reactions. It said that scientists cannot be sure that all food additives are safe because not enough is known about how they react in the body with chemicals, pesticides and insecticide residues, prescription drugs, cosmetics and other foods. I firmly believe the Canadian consumer has the right to know what a drug product contains, be it prescription or non-prescription, when they buy it or use it. This applies to all drug products which are taken internally.
A drug is not dangerous on the store or pharmacy shelf but it can be potentially dangerous when taken by a person who cannot tolerate certain substances. Studies have shown that people do read labels in order to avoid undesirable components in products. People do experience serious side effects and severe allergic reactions. Some such adverse effects could have been avoided had the person had the opportunity to read the label on the medication and find a pharmaceutical product without the agent they need to avoid.
I must pause here and give credit to the key organization responsible for my presentation of this motion for debate. The Allergy Information Association made available to me extensive material and documentation on reactions to various
substances. Normally 1 would not actively call attention to an organization. However, in this instance I believe it is important for me to set out in Hansard the address of this organization so that many people who suffer from various allergies or low tolerances to certain substances can contact the association for assistance and support. The Allergy Information Association is located at 25 Poynter Drive, Suite 7, Weston, Ontario, M9R 1 K8, telephone (416) 244-8585. I do not want this to sound like a commercial but I believe many Canadians will appreciate knowing of this association if they have or suffer from allergic reactions.
In giving credit to the A1A I should also point out that this motion touches me closely personally. As many of my colleagues know, I am the father of young twins. Unfortunately they suffer from many allergies to various substances. My wife and I have spent many restless days and nights trying various prescription medications to determine those which the children could tolerate and those to which they had a reaction. If the information was readily available, it could have saved us a lot of suffering. My son is also asthmatic, which further complicates the use of medication.
I would also like to give a great deal of credit to Dr. Ed Napke, chief of the Product Related Disease Division, Bureau of Epidemiology, Health Protection Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare. Dr. Napke provided a great deal of information in preparation for today. He has been working in this field for 20 years and 1 consider his expertise and knowledge of great benefit in addressing this issue. I would particularly like to use a quotation of his which is:
Man is a walking test-tube. Each time a chemical is added or subtracted the
balance may be upset.
This statement seems to validate beyond question my argument for the passage of this motion.
1 should start with a simple definition of a drug. A drug is any substance of therapeutic, diagnostic or prophylactic indication, including medical devices and objects such as an IUCD. An adverse reaction is any action which is not of therapeutic, diagnostic or prophylactic benefit to the patient. I must also define the term "excipient". Medications are composed of two types of ingredients, usually termed the active and non-active. The active ingredients are, for therapeutic purposes, the raison d'etre of the drug. The inactive ingredients are more properly called excipients. They are those things used as coaters, binders, fillers, colourings and flavourings. They were originally termed inactive because they were considered inert, not adding to or affecting the intended action of the active ingredient.
The actual incidence of adverse drug reactions in the general population is not known. The incidence in the institutionalized population has been obtained from surveys of hospitalized patients where the prevalence ranges from 6 per cent to 15 per cent. In addition, 3 per cent of admissions to acute care hospitals are attributed to adverse drug reactions. Fatal drug reactions are, thankfully, quite rare.
August 18, 1987

I would have liked nothing better than to come to this House this afternoon prepared with specific numbers of Canadians who have suffered or been treated for an adverse reaction to either a prescribed or non-prescribed drug. I would like to have come prepared with exact cost figures indicating the amount of money adverse drug reactions cost the Canadian taxpayer each year. These figures would have made the Government and my colleagues realize the seriousness of this motion. Unfortunately, it is almost impossible to obtain such data.
It is indeed sad that adverse drug reactions are not well identified and, when they are, are not well reported or analysed as to their bases. While I give credit to the federal Government in studying the various aspects of adverse reactions through the adverse reaction program of the Health Protection Branch, it is more and more evident that more needs to be done. The incidence of drug adverse reactions in hospital patients varies, according to the intensity of monitoring, from a low of 5 per cent to a high of 35 per cent. As many as 5 per cent of monitored patients may suffer from drug adverse reactions, or DAR, on admission to hospital, while more than 3.5 per cent of in-hospital deaths have been drug attributed. Those figure were taken from an article published more than 10 years ago. It is highly possible that the number is higher now because our society seems to be using more and more drugs.
In recent years it has been established that at least some adverse drug reactions are caused by the excipient rather than the therapeutic ingredient. Therefore it is important that the Government take action to require the labelling of all drugs which would include a quantitative list of all medical and nonmedical ingredients. In other words, the label would contain both the active and excipient ingredients.
1 can quote specific medical cases here but it would prove pointless unless everyone listening had a medical background. 1 see one or two doctors, but they are in the minority.
