speechtext:
The onus seems to be on persons suffering the allergy, reaction or low tolerance to a substance to determine which products they can and cannot consume. The labelling of food has made this easier and much safer. The labelling of all drugs will have the same impact. It will make the choice easier and safer for the consumer and patient.
To bring this debate to a non-medical level let me say that colouring agents are probably the best studied and most common causes of adverse reactions in excipients. As well, one of the most common food allergens is milk. Many people, including one of my twins during the early stages, suffered from a lactose intolerance. Corn is also a common element causing an allergic reaction. Both these substances are often used as fillers in various medications.
Food and Drug Regulations
Many pharmaceutical products contain the gluten of wheat, usually as an inert excipient in capsules, tablets and suspensions. 1 am listing here but a few of the more well known substances which cause reactions in many Canadians. There are many others used in many products, but their names may not be so familiar.
Polyethylene glycol is used in many drugs and in products such as shaving lotions and milk shakes. Alcohols in pharmaceuticals are inappropriate for patients such as children and alcoholics. Alcohol is known to produce a synergistic effect with other medication. Therefore, an alcohol-containing medication should not be taken in conjunction with a medication which interacts with alcohol. Since the content of alcohol in medications is unknown, adverse reactions and lack of therapeutic benefit can result.
Celiac disease is a condition whereby wheat, rye, barley and oats and their products cannot be tolerated by the body. As drugs have fillers, it is important to know what the drug contains on the outside as a coating as well as in the inside as medication. I am fortunate enough to have become aware of this disease through the Edmonton Celiac Association.
The public is now aware of the fatal association of aspirin- acetylsalicylic acid-and Reye's syndrome. The public is probably not aware that many medications contain acetylsalicylic acid as an ingredient.
Many drug products have propylene glycol as their solvents. How many other "active ingredients" are stigmatized as causing or being associated with hypertension, cardiovascular collapse or even sudden, unexplained fatal reactions? The list is unknown since far too often the full formulation of the product is unknown except to the individual manufacturer and a few governmental drug agencies.
Similarly, metabisulphite, a common preservative in Canada in food, drink and drugs, has been found to cause acute asthmatic attacks in chronic asthmatics. More recently this preservative, used in certain intravenous products, has caused respiratory arrest in patients. Presently, inasmuch as these compounds are classified as "inactive", manufacturers are not required to list them on the product label. This makes it virtually impossible for a person to know whether he will have a reaction to a certain medication even if that person knows he or she has a low tolerance level or allergic reaction to a specific substance.
Information concerning the occurrence of these common additives in medications is virtually impossible to obtain. Specifications of dyes, preservatives, fillers, binders, lubricants, glidants, disintegrants, coatings, flavourings and sweeteners, is lacking. The care of patients sensitive to excipients is far more difficult without information on these additives.
The excipients and additives in drug formulations have been described as inert because they do not have an active role in the prevention or treatment of particular ailments. This has led

August 18, 1987
Food and Drug Regulations
to the misconception among physicians, pharmacists, drug manufacturers and the public that they are harmless and unworthy of mention. In fact, pharmacists are allowed to substitute drug formulations without regard to the excipients as long as they ensure that the active ingredients in the substitutions are the same as those in the formulation prescribed.
The Canadian public deserves to be better protected. The United States has legislation requiring complete labelling of some food, drugs and cosmetics that incorporate more than one ingredient no matter how innocuous the constituents are believed to be. 1 refer not to voting constituents this time, Mr. Speaker.
In Canada drug manufacturers are not even required to share this information with physicians or pharmacists when they introduce a new drug or reformulate a product already being marketed. Nor are pharmacists required to disclose the contents of formulations which they prepare in the absence of commercially available products.
The third stream of activity that has contributed to physicians and the paramedical professions not knowing or being aware of the product formulations is industry. Industry in the past has refused to reveal its formulations and know-how to the professions for a very good reason, namely, rivalry in business. However, with modern techniques most trade secrets can soon be unravelled whilst others can be patented. Therefore, the complete formulation should be made known to the health professionals and the general public.
In fact, the Government's Bill C-22 will provide much greater patent protection for the pharmaceutical industry and, unknowingly, the Bill actually strengthens the argument for my motion.
At one time the pharmacist and the physician did know what the excipients were in a product. There once was a time when pharmacists compounded the product and could, with some reasonable assurance, tell physicians what their patients received chemically as far as that product was concerned. Today that is not the case.
The modern pharmacist, for all his declared interest in becoming a drug information expert, often has very little knowledge, or none, of the excipients, colouring matter, particle size, et cetera, which make up a particular drug product. How can he? Sometimes even the manufacturer does not know for the manufacturer may be using a colorant or other additive which was purchased under trade name from another firm. This makes a very strong case indeed in support of the labelling of all ingredients for drugs.
One very important point in this debate-perhaps the most important factor over-all-is that the patient is at multiple risk. He suffers an ill effect, an "active" ingredient is consequently denied him and, on the other hand, a non-active ingredient which is the unsuspected culprit may show up again in the next medication he receives and produce the same
unwanted reaction once more. It is conceivable that the patient might be denied proper treatment because of his reactions to unknown ingredients.
The key element in this entire speech is that it is impossible to trace or test for allergic reactions or to treat for allergy without a complete list of excipients. The medical profession cannot treat a patient when they do not know what substances compose a drug and they cannot determine an allergic reaction to a product when they do not know what the product contains.
During the month of June there was a great deal of debate in this House on the issue of unborn foetuses. In this regard it is important to note that the developing foetus or neonatal individual is particularly susceptible to the toxic effects of drugs and other chemicals. The foetus is the unwilling recipient of whatever the mother ingests, inhales or applies to the skin.
More recent studies have confirmed a continuing high drug use during pregnancy. One study reported that women took an average of 15.6 drugs during the course of their pregnancies. This figure represents 6.4 prescription drugs and 3.2 over the counter medications during the pregnancy and six additional drugs during labour and delivery. Despite public awareness of the tragedies associated with drugs such as thalidomide and alcohol, the publicity warning pregnant women to avoid the unnecessary use of drugs during pregnancy has been ineffective.
In closing, I should note that for the manufacture of a new drug identification number Canadian drug regulations require that all submissions contain a quantitative list of ingredients including colouring agents. Although such information is regarded as confidential, the Health Protection Branch has been instrumental in bringing the consumer, physician and manufacturer together in difficult cases. This work by the HPB is to be commended but it certainly does not go far enough.
1 am certain every Member in this House has many constituents who suffer from allergies, whether to certain drugs or certain foods. This motion, while directly benefiting a minority in Canada, will indirectly benefit each and every Canadian by enabling the consumer to make the best choice with the greatest amount of relevant information. I urge all Members of this House to support the motion.

August 18, 1987

I believe that often it is that kind of specific initiative that forces Governments, of whatever political stripe, to change something.
Unfortunately, it is too often left to some abstract individuals to develop policies, from some building in Ottawa or Hull, on the sixth floor, and often those people do not have specific field experience or are not aware of the impact.
First, 1 think it would be important to explain the thrust of the motion: it would urge the Government to bring in amendments such that each drug is labelled with a list of all ingredients. Currently medicinal ingredients are listed, but all the non-medicinal ingredients in that drug should be listed so as to inform people of the impact the drug they are taking could have on someone suffering from allergies.
On the other hand, as I told the Hon. Member earlier when he enumerated a series of learned terms only used by doctors because of their training and written on the labels of drug containers and boxes, the vocabulary used by doctors is of no help to the layman.
I therefore believe that the Hon. Member should ask that the labels for every drug include directions for use not only in technical or medical terms, but also in terms that can be understood by the public.
I believe that we should take this opportunity to ensure that all information given on pharmaceutical or food products, and this include dosage, directions for use and ingredients, be printed in large readable characters. There are thousands of senior citizens in Canada who have to take medication because of age or illness, but unfortunately, to save money, the drug companies write the directions for use in virtually unreadable print.
1 am in full agreement with the motion of the Hon. Member. If we do not force companies to make their directions easy to read, we shall not meet our objective. I believe however that we should add to the motion that directions for use should be written not only in understandable terms, but also in easy to read characters.
Mr. Speaker, I trust that this motion will receive the support of all Members of this House and that it will be agreed to as quickly as possible because, as the Hon. Member has shown, some companies are saying that they are against such an amendment as their formula could then be copied by competitors. We know what it means when people are afraid of being copied! Others say that it would be too costly. I find this unacceptable.
The first duty of Parliament must be to protect the life, health and welfare of the public. We can think about the cost later. These companies are making a lot of money. It is unacceptable that we, Members of the House of Commons, whatever our political stripe, should give in to blackmail for monetary reasons.
Food and Drug Regulations
I somebody needs a drug, it is a matter of life and death. A healthy person does not need any drugs. But when someone has to take a drug, it is important to make sure that that drug will improve his or her health, and that it will contribute to cure the disease or ease the pain related to it, but without having adverse effects on people who suffer from allergies.
I will conclude on this, Mr. Speaker, because I feel that the debate will not last very long if we all agree, given that the Conservative Member . . . until we have proof to the contrary, I believe that the New Democrats will also be in agreement. On this side, we feel it is useless to go on with this debate and 1 am prepared to pass this motion right away. Let us act. 1 congragulate once more the Hon. Member. If his motion is passed rapidly and if we succeed in forcing those companies to change, we might save human lives and avoid many sufferings.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my loquacious Liberal colleague has intimated that perhaps it is unnecessary for a member of the New Democratic Party to speak because, of course, the NDP, being a Party that represents the enlightened average Canadian, would surely support a Bill of such eminent merit, as it is. It is a motion that is long past due.
The principle that the consumer should be made aware of the contents of what he or she purchases for consumption is an elementary principle that is particularly critical when it involves drugs and medicines.
The Member has suggested that inert ingredients be labelled. Before addressing that specific aspect of his proposition, perhaps he should also give attention to the fact that the consumer who goes to a drugstore to receive a prescription generally gets a little bottle with the date of the prescription, perhaps the contents, the frequency of intake, and perhaps even the size of the dose.
I would suggest that in addition to labelling and making available the inert contents of a drug or pharmaceutical, the time is long past due when a patient should know what the pharmacist and the doctor know, which is the specific characteristics of the drug in terms of its effectiveness, its appropriate dosage, its likely side effects; in terms of its potential toxicity, in terms of its incompatibility with other drugs that might be taken, and any other limitations on the use of a particular drug that would be of importance in protecting the health of an individual.
I hope that the Hon. Member, in considering the provision of the contents of a medicine with respect to excipients, would also address the need for the complete availability of all pertinent information with respect to a pharmaceutical. We know that the druggist gets the information from the original package and a great deal of information is available to the doctor. I believe it also ought to be available to patients.

August 18, 1987
Food and Drug Regulations
It is hard to imagine any drug that does not have some degree of toxicity, or limitations in terms of incompatibilities with other agents that might be consumed. It is rare to find an antibiotic or chemotherapeutic agent that does not have those limitations. Perhaps only penicillin can be classified as a commonly used drug that has no significant toxicity. But penicillin is a drug that suggests an element which is often not taken cognizance of in drugs as well as in agents. It is the idiosyncratic reaction of individuals to a variety of agencies. In other words, penicillin causes allergies, as people know.
As the Hon. Member has identified, there are a great many other ingredients that have nothing to do with the therapeutic properties of a drug but are included for a variety of reasons, such as colour, filler, binding agents, and to provide a pleasant taste.
These agents, if not identified, have the potential of causing the same kinds of effects in terms of drugs as the sulphates had with respect to food. Since the majority of us are not susceptible to these idiosyncratic reactions, too little attention has been paid to the potential danger that exists for a relative few. Because it is related to such a relative few, it should not at all be cause for lessening our concern. I was impressed by the reference made by the Hon. Member to his personal experiences and the experiences of his family with respect to a variety of substances. 1 would say to him that just over the last couple of weeks my family and I have become aware of allergic reactions which have caused a serious impediment to the activities of two of my children. The late recognition of these idiosyncrasies has caused my children considerable difficulty.
It is with congratulations and felicitations that I rise to support the Hon. Member in proposing this resolution. It is a resolution, as the previous speaker from the Liberal Party indicated, that all Members of this House, all three Parties, should be capable of supporting. The implementation of this legislation should be prepared as quickly as possible.
I will not prolong the debate so we may have an opportunity to vote positively on this motion. I would like to express my appreciation once more for having the opportunity to support this motion.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FOOD AND DRUG REGULATIONS SUGGESTED DRUG CONTENT LABELLING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to deal with an issue which is amongst the priorities set by the Government of Canada in the field of health care. I am referring to the labelling of drugs and more precisely to the listing of the medicinal and non-medicinal ingredients they may contain.
In its 1986 publication entitled Achieving Health for all: a framework for Health Promotion, the Government of Canada identifies three areas which are poorly covered by existing
health policies and practices. The first one is prevention on which we should put greater emphasis. Various preventable diseases and injuries continue to jeopardize the health and quality of life of Canadians.
Even though most Canadians are unaffected, some nonmedicinal ingredients have been incriminated in benign or serious side effects, especially various forms of allergies.
Mr. Speaker, some non-medicinal ingredients may be used routinely in pharmaceutical products for safety reasons or for effectiveness. For example, an ingredient may be used to prevent tablets from crumbling or to maintain the sterility of a product. Others may promote the release of the active ingredient in the body after ingestion or help maintain the potency of that ingredient.
In general, non-medicinal ingredients have no detectable effect on the people taking the drug. However, in the last few years, health professionals and regulatory agencies have started to observe that some groups of Canadians show a degree of intolerance or allergy to certain ingredients.
Mr. Speaker, reports on such reactions show considerable variations. Among the most extreme I could mention a few cases of anaphylaxis, some of them followed by death. However, the responsible ingredient is seldom identified. Beside causing direct anaphylaxis, some non-medicinal ingredients have been reported to be the cause of strain-induced anaphylaxis.
Fatigue, nervousness and headaches are typical examples of symptoms related to reactions caused by non-medicinal ingredients ranking at the bottom of the scale with respect to health hazards.
A wide variety of chemical products used as non-medicinal ingredients in drugs are also added to some foods. When explaining the details of symptoms noticed in conjunction with some of these substances, I will be more specific about their more widespread use as food additives.
Sodium metabisulphite and similar compounds were often found in fruit juices, wine and beer; these substances were also sprayed on mushrooms, vegetables, potato chips and seafoods to maintain their flavour and preserve them longer. Being an oxidizing agent, bisulphite removes the oxygen required for bacterial growth and thus prevents deterioration. This is why sodium metabisulphite would also be sprayed on freshly-prepared salads in restaurants and on grocery stores fruits and vegetables stands to keep them fresh. It has been ascertained that swallowing metabisulphite may cause vomiting, skin rashes and, sometimes, congestive breath, high blood pressure and respiratory problems. However there is no explanation for the precise mechanism of reactions to metabisulphite.
It is known that monosodic glutamate, an additive often used with Chinese food, will cause wheezing respiration in some asthmatic patients. For other sensitive persons it will lead to numbness of the back of the neck, facial tension, thoracic pain and difficult breathing. Sensitive subjects showed
August 18, 1987

symptoms of the syndrome after ingesting up to three grams of MSG.
In one study, benzoates, butylated hydroxytoluene and butylated hydroxyanisole, were incriminated, respectively, in 11 and 1 5 per cent of chronic and recurrent skin rashes. These preservatives are often present in prepared foods, bread, powdered milk and potato flakes. It is hard to believe, Mr. Speaker, that the food we normally eat contains substances with such complicated names. The same preservatives are also found in fats, oil, margarine, mayonnaise, jam, chocolate, soft drinks and powdered beverage mixes. Although seldom causing gastro-intestinal symptoms, nitrates and nitrites have been blamed in cases of cyanosis in babies who were fed spinach.
Clearly, Mr. Speaker, the range of side effects is very extensive, even if only a small proportion of Canadians seem to have adverse reactions to some of these ingredients. Nor is there any doubt that some of these additives are widely used in our society and do not cause any obvious problems for most Canadians. Because of the wide variety of chemicals used in drugs available in Canada, it is impossible to eliminate completely non-medicinal ingredients from all products.
For instance, some non-medicinal ingredients are essential to prevent the growth of bacteria, fungi, and algae in medication. Granted, some Canadians may have adverse reactions associated with such substances. However, when a substitute non-medicinal ingredient cannot be found, we must not forget that various toxins released by bacteria, fungi and algae have been associated with serious intestinal, and sometimes even neurological, symptoms.
Sulphite is one of the remarquable non-medicinal ingredients which have been used in food and drugs. Mr. Speaker, I want to emphasize that though it is impossible to eliminate it from all pharmaceutical products, its use in foods is not considered essential. Last October, the Government of Canada, therefore, limited the use of sulphites in fresh food, such as salad preparations in restaurants.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, since it is impossible to replace or eliminate all non-medicinal ingredients from all drugs, steps have been taken to protect Canadians from being uselessly exposed to non-medicinal ingredients to which they know they are sensitive or allergic. This is in fact an avoidable risk factor. In this connection, I have been advised that the Health Protection Branch has been concerned for a number of years by the presence of non-medicinal ingredients in drugs.
Approximately two years ago, associations of pharmaceutical manufacturers adopted voluntary guidelines concerning the disclosure of potentially dangerous non-medicinal ingredients. The manufacturers of prescription drugs have agreed to disclose the presence of those ingredients which had been clearly associated with symptoms of intolerance or allergy among certain patients. This disclosure has been made to the Canadian Pharmaceutical Association for inclusion in the descriptions of drugs which appear in the reference book
Food and Drug Regulations
entitled "Compendium of Pharmaceutical and Specialties". As to the makers of over-the-counter drugs, they have accepted to indicate the presence of non-medicinal ingredients on their labels.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, these measures reflect both our concern for and our monitoring of the useless exposure of Canadian men and women to non-medicinal ingredients which their systems just cannot tolerate. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, these measures are only an example of the concerted commitment of the regulating agencies, the health professionals and drug manufacturers to enhancing prevention in health care.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find myself somewhat uncomfortable this afternoon speaking to the motion of the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Dorin). I wish to give him a great deal of credit for the fact that he has brought this matter to the attention of the House and, more particularly, to the attention of the Government, although 1 have some fears that the Government is not as receptive to the idea as I might like to think it should be. I dare say that there are some problems that need to be worked out with respect to this matter.
1 wish to commend the Hon. Member since he has done an excellent job of presenting the problems that exist now for many people in the country who have cause to take a drug of some form and find that they have an idiosyncratic or an allergic reaction to it. I would have preferred, had I had any influence in the wording of the motion, to expand it since 1 continually come across products at my home that are bought from the drug store, the grocery store or the hardware store, be they liquids, solids or powders, which absolutely fail to mention on their labels what is in them. That is just as dangerous because if a child takes one of those products we have no way of knowing whether or not it is a dangerous product. There may be a warning printed on the product, for example, "Danger If Ingested", "Do Not Ingest" or "Keep Away From Children", but these warnings do not tell us what the actual ingredients are. That is the real hazard we should be addressing. The motion is extremely timely, but it needs to be expanded to other products which are not deemed to be drugs.
I was particularly interested in the personal references that the Hon. Member for Edmonton West made inasmuch as two of them struck a particular note with me in a personal manner as well. First, he mentioned his farpous twins. We certainly want to congratulate him on his young family by way of twins. I am interested in those twins, too, because I have heard about them and a bit about their problems since one of their babysitters is a girl who worked in my office here in Ottawa for several years. I know that she is very fond of those twins and is concerned about the problems they have by way of allergies.

August 18, 1987
Food and Drug Regulations
The Hon. Member referred to consultations that he has had with one of the officials in the Department who is in charge of the adverse reaction program, Dr. Ed Napke. Interestingly enough, Dr. Napke and I were class-mates at the University of Toronto Medical School a number of years ago. We have all enjoyed Dr. Napke's humour over the years and the very serious approach he takes to adverse drug reactions. I want to commend him for the work that he has done on behalf of the Department in this area. I think it likely that if we had a chance to talk to Dr. Napke further we would probably find that he is very sympathetic to many of the proposals included in the Hon. Member's motion.
I was also interested in the presentation made by the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy). He and I have occasion to sit together on the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare. I have a great deal of respect for the contributions he makes to the deliberations of our committee. Today, for instance, he talked about the need for patients to have more information about drugs. To a large extent I think that he is right. On the other hand, as a practising physician, I would say that in the past I have never hesitated to provide a patient with the very kind of information he wants to have with respect to the adverse effects of a drug, what the synergistic effects may be with other drugs and so on. I think people are entitled to that information, although 1 have some reservation about providing it to every patient unless he or she particularly asks for it, because there are anxieties that can be produced in people if they read all the details about the adverse reports that have been documented on any given drug. However, 1 think the Hon. Member's contribution was very useful and I commend him for it.
Having said that, I am sure that there are some problems with the motion before the House. I wish to touch on those briefly. They are probably sufficient not to allow it to be passed today. I encourage the Hon. Member not to let this issue die. I think it is a very fundamental issue. He and the people who are interested in allergies with whom he has consulted have a valid concern.
I remind the Hon. Member and the House that there are other ways of pursuing this matter. In the Hon. Member's case we should undoubtedly see this issue brought before our caucus committee on health. There is no reason why the Hon. Member could not present this issue before those of us in our caucus who are interested in health care issues. There is no reason that he should not make representation to the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare to ask it to consider discussing it at the level of the standing committee. Failing that, as a Member of Parliament he has a right to attend the meeting of the standing committee at which the Minister himself is present to answer for his Estimates. If I were the chairman of that committee I would want to see the Hon. Member recognized to have a chance to ask questions in this regard. I think that is a very legitimate use of the standing committee.
Having said that, there are some matters concerning this issue that are of concern to the Government. I suppose they should be put on the floor at this time. The disclosure of nonmedicinal ingredients is considered to be a solution to the problem. However, it should be interpreted in light of the full problem. The determination of which agent or agents which someone may be sensitive to is often an elusive process. This is particularly true for allergic reactions involving the gastrointestinal tract. This system, unlike other systems in the body, is relatively inaccessible as compared to organs such as the skin and it is therefore hard to see reactions. Thus, a patient's symptoms of intolerance may be heightened or modified by reactions to other substances to which concurrent exposure has occurred. These substances may be airborne, ingested or have come into contact with a patient's skin. In fact, all three modes of contact may occur simultaneously.
The whole issue of the diagnosis of what is an allergic reaction and what the allergen or cause of it may be, also is compounded or confounded, one might use either word, by the placebo effect. I wish to touch upon that for a moment.
This well documented syndrome revolves around the erroneous attribution of symptoms to some particular chemical food or circumstance of events. In this case, the presumed cause is incorrect and cannot be scientifically demonstrated to have an effect. This agent is termed a placebo. To appreciate fully the magnitude of the placebo effect, and, therefore, the gravity of its implications, I wish to summarize briefly the scope of the scientifically documented medical effects of placebos.
Almost any type of pain may respond to placebos: pain after surgery, pain during and after childbirth, dental pain, and the distress of cancer. In the treatment of 150 patients with headaches caused by tension, the common cold, sinusitis, premenstrual tension, and eye strain, one investigator found that placebos relieved pain completely in 43 per cent of cases, and partially in another 31 per cent. Others have come to similar conclusions. Cough, insomnia, seasickness, chronic bronchitis, and the common cold may all yield to the placebo. Patients with osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis have shown improvement. In some studies stomach ulcers, stomach irritation, and heartburn have shown amelioration after placebo administration in 92 per cent of patients. This showing was so impressive that certain gastroenterologists have speculated on whether most of the hundreds of older "treatments" for ulcers were not primarily placebo remedies.
Other aspects of body function such as blood pressure and sputum production, have also displayed a change due to a placebo. In the classic Cornell studies on one subject who had a serious stomach problem, placebos and manipulation of psychological beliefs produced impressive changes in the appearance and motility of the stomach lining, and in the secretion of gastric juice. The same investigators were able to prevent vomiting from an emetic in a pregnant woman by
August 18, 1987

assuring her that this nauseating drug would actually relieve the excess vomiting from which she suffered.
In Boston, dental student volunteers produced increased amounts of saliva when they were given water that was suggested to be sour, and they showed a decrease in flow when citric acid was given with the suggestion that it was tasteless.
To the great surprise of two researchers in Surrey, England, the incontinence of "deteriorated" psychotic patients changed dramatically for the better when the patients were given sugar pills three times a day. Similar results were observed in a study in Maryland of schizophrenic and senile patients.
I would add my own anecdotal observation as a physician, in my early days when we dispensed drugs from our own office, people with certain types of pain would tell us that the aspirin they had taken had no effect at all. We would give them a brown coloured aspirin and they might find complete relief or they may have taken a pink aspirin and received no relief at all. This placebo effect is very important when one is trying to assess the effect of drugs on patients. It is very readily demonstrable.
On the other hand, the placebo also has the capacity for producing many types of adverse effects. While most side effects after a placebo are hard to measure, such as nausea, thirst, headache, dizziness, sleepiness, insomnia, fatigue, depression, numbness, difficulty in concentrating, hallucinations, feelings of cold or warmth, itching, and the like, some side effects are of the kind that are verifiable by the observer. These include vomiting, tremor, fast heart beat, diarrhea, changes in blood pressure, pallor, skin rashes of alarming severity, hives, unsteadiness of gait, and swelling.
Two prominent researchers described three major reactions to placebos in 31 patients engaged in a clinical trial. One had sudden, overwhelming weakness, palpitation, and nausea within 15 minutes of taking a placebo. A second patient developed a diffuse, itchy red rash which was diagnosed by a dermatologist as a typical dermatitis from drugs. The third patient had repeated reactions within 10 minutes of taking the pills that included abdominal pain, watery diarrhea, skin rashes, and swelling of the lips.
In another study a patient who had travelled to Miami on holiday called his physician to complain that his medicine had so weakened him as to cause a near drowning accident in the surf. A hasty check of the records showed that the patient was taking a placebo.
One could go on and give further evidence of the peculiar effects of placebos, and the involvement that this strange phenomenon has on the whole taking of drugs. I can appreciate why some of our officials in the Government are loath, at this time, to see a full blown acceptance of the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Edmonton West.
In closing, I would certainly encourage him not to put this to rest and to make sure that he comes back with this motion again, either to committee or to the House. I compliment him
Food and Drug Regulations
for the effort that he has put into his presentation to the House today.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FOOD AND DRUG REGULATIONS SUGGESTED DRUG CONTENT LABELLING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first,
I wish to congratulate my colleague for Edmonton West (Mr. Dorin) on his motion.
Mr. Speaker, the presence of non-medicinal ingredients in drugs is always a source of concern for the Canadian Government.
It is quite usual for non-medicinal ingredients to be added in various concentrations to pharmaceutical products sold on the market to increase their safety and effectiveness. Some of these non-medicinal ingredients keep the drug active while others delay micro-biological contamination. Many of these drugs are sold in Canada, each with its own physical and chemical properties which must be taken into account in determining the dosage appropriate to the patient and his state of health.
While most of these non-medicinal ingredients can be consumed without apparent ill effect by most patients under treatment, a limited number of them have been associated with adverse side effects. The ingredients most often mentioned in such cases include sulfites, tartrazines, parabens, gluten, sugars and alcohols. For technical reasons, it is impossible to eliminate consistently all these ingredients from all drugs. Indeed, in some cases, their absence could reduce the availability of the drugs themselves.
Mr. Speaker, although a policy aimed at eliminating these non-medicinal products from all Canadian-made drugs cannot possibly protect sub-groups of Canadians against all risks of undesirable secondary effects, we must not forget that the Department of National Health and Welfare's Health Protection Branch requires that all pharmaceutical products be tested before they are marketed in this country, and that drugs so tested must contain all non-medicinal ingredients that will be added to the product sold to the public.
Checking the acceptability of a new drug makes it possible to control the harmlessness and efficiency of any non-medicinal ingredients it may include. In addition, about two years ago the associations of drug manufacturers voluntarily decided to establish guidelines concerning the disclosure of nonmedicinal ingredients. Manufacturers of prescription drugs agreed to make public the non-medicinal ingredients most commonly associated with reactions of intolerance, and they conveyed this information to the Canadian Pharmaceutical Association. For their part, manufacturers of unrestricted drugs agreed to list on labels all non-medicinal ingredients contained in their products.
There is no doubt that health professionals, drug manufacturers and regulating agencies in this sector in Canada have combined their efforts in the interest of our population.

August 18, 1987
Adjournment Debate
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to commend all parties involved in this endeavour. The tables prepared by the Canadian Pharmaceutical Association are a telling example of the role which professional associations have voluntarily agreed to play. One of the first priorities of our health care system is to make Canadians increasingly aware of the various types of illnesses and injuries they might be able to avoid. Prevention means that such factors as may lead to an undesirable condition must first be identified, and then reduced or eliminated. In this context, Mr. Speaker, the spirit of co-operation which has been the hallmark of Canada's intervention with respect to non-medicinal ingredients attests to our commitment to lay even more emphasis on prevention within our health care system.

Mr. Speaker, on May 14 the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight), in a communique related to changes to be made in the Indian post-secondary education program, made the following statement:
Education and training are important tools in today's technological society. They are even more important for Indian people in the process of developing self-government and economic self-reliance.
1 agree entirely with what the Minister said in that communique. In another interesting document entitled "A Framework for Diversification in Western Canada" we read the following on page 9:
Over time the greatest returns to Canada will result from an investment in our people. Education and training, while broadly a provincial responsibility, is of special interest to the federal Government both with respect to highly qualified workers and to native people. The federal Government is anxious to see this nation's current performance improved in these areas.
The Indian post-secondary education program has been a huge success. It certainly is the avenue which leads Indian and Inuit people from social assistance to economic independence, from welfare to personal well-being, self-respect, and selfsufficiency.
That being so, I would ask the House why there is such a schizophrenic response to the delivery of these valuable programs. I want the House and the country to know that there has been a severe capping of one of the most successful and one of the most important federal government programs in existence.
I also want the House to know what is the Minister's case. The Minister's case is that the participation rate of this program has grown. Ten years ago there were 3,500 eligible students in this Indian post-secondary education program, and today there are 12,000. The costs have grown from $8 million to S93.7 million. That is the beginning and that is the end of the Minister's case.
I want to tell the House that that is no case at all, because it does not say anything about inflation over those years. It does not say anything about the growing demand which must be met for reasons the Minister himself has given. It does not say anything at all about the fact that Indian and Inuit people are rapidly taking control over their own lives.
In that same communique the Minister said that education and training remained a priority for him. At the same time, applications for assistance under this program are to be considered on a very strict priority basis.
I cannot take the time of the House to go through all the priorities, but I want the House to know that out of the five categories described by the Minister, only categories one and two-that is, Indian and Inuit students who were enrolled in 1986-87 and are continuing on in 1987-88, and students whose applications for assistance were deferred in 1986-87-will be funded out of this allocation advanced by the Minister and approved by Parliament.
Who will be left out? Eligible high school graduates are to be left out. Mature students who are enrolling in postsecondary education for the first time are to be left out. Would you believe it, sir, that students enrolling in programs for the LL B, the law degree, for the MD, the medical degree, or for the bachelor of education degree are to be left out? If along the way one of these students in any program has dropped out and wants to return, he will have no chance at all of getting back. Those are the priorities. This means that a large number of students will be turned away.
Let me quote from the Debates of the other place. Senator Len Marchand, himself an Indian person, has said the following:
In my home band alone, which consists of 900 to 1,000 members, there are 26 students who will not receive funding for post-secondary education this fall.
From talking with members of other bands around the country, I have learned that there are literally going to be hundreds, or a few thousand, of students who will not be able to pursue post-secondary education this fall. I call this a disastrous policy.
I just learned that a very fine cultural college in Hobbema, Alberta, the Maskwachees Cultural College, has already in the
August 18, 1987

month of August had to turn down 31 applications for this program.
At this very moment, on the Alexander Reserve in Alberta, an emergency meeting is being held, attended by grassroots educational leaders who are members of the Indian community or serve the Indian community. They call the current situation a crisis. It is a crisis because we know that there is a clear link between education and future employment and economic development. There is a clear link between education and aboriginal self-government.
The Government talks about economic development, believing that it is the most important route for Indian people. It talks about Indian self-government. It uses the terminology and the phraseology. I want to tell the House and the country, however, that the Government uses all the right words, but it denies the substance thereof. I call upon the Minister to take dramatic action to show that his priorities are real and that education for Indian and Inuit students will not be denied but that this program will be met to the fullest possible extent.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to rise on behalf of the Minister to respond to my friend, the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner). He has raised an interesting question. It is certainly the case that the Indian post-secondary education assistance program established by the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs is unique.
As the Hon. Member indicated, the budget for the program has grown substantially, from $8 million a decade ago to $93.7 million in 1987-88. Over the same period, the number of fulltime equivalent students has increased from roughly 3,500 to approximately 12,000.
I would like to highlight the major provisions of this program which has the goal of enabling Indian access to postsecondary education. Full-time students can receive financial assistance for undergraduate, masters and doctoral programs, community college diplomas and college-entrance preparation courses. The costs of tuition, books, supplies and transportation for students and dependents is covered, together with living allowances of from $120 to $184 a week, shelter and child care allowances and a special incentive for graduate students. The funding is provided as a grant; there is no loan component nor is there a means test.
This year's increased budget will mean that most of the students applying for assistance will receive it. A priority system ensures fairness and consistency in approving applications. Students who are continuing their post-secondary education programs must have first draw on the budget. This includes students who were enrolled in undergraduate programs last year and who will be enrolling in graduate programs or professional degree programs in 1987-88. Next are those who were deferred last year for lack of funds.
Adjournment Debate
In order to provide additional access to post-secondary studies, the Department's next priorities are new undergraduate and college entrants and college preparation students. Students who are beginning post-graduate studies or studies toward a second professional degree and who were not enrolled in post-secondary studies last year have been given a lower priority.
To assist individuals in achieving their personal career potential and strengthen the process of self-government and devolution of programs to bands, we must provide the opportunity within government resources for post-secondary education. The Department is now reviewing other options for student assistance and special post-secondary programs and will be discussing these with Indian leaders in the months ahead.

subtopic: EXTERNAL. AFFAIRS-NICARAGUA-REPORTED BANNING OF CONSERVATIVE PARTY-ACCESS TO POLITICAL PRISONERS

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EXTERNAL. AFFAIRS-NICARAGUA-REPORTED BANNING OF CONSERVATIVE PARTY-ACCESS TO POLITICAL PRISONERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 5 I rose in this House to ask a question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) regarding a situation in Nicaragua that was of great concern to me. Two months previously I, as chairman of the Canadian section of the IPU, along with others, visited Nicaragua. I had looked forward with some anticipation to determining the level of pluralism in that country. President Ortega assured us that pluralism was alive and well. However, there were a number of signs in that country at that time which indicated that was not true at all.
When we got back in June, we heard that the chairman of the Conservative Party had been put under house arrest and subsequently released, but that his Party had been banned.
Since that time we have seen some very promising developments in Central America. The recent proposal to bring about peace in that troubled part of the world seems to be gathering momentum. The President of the United States has made a proposal as well and has looked with some favour at least on the other proposal. I hope, and I think all Members of the House will agree, that these negotiations will bear fruit and that there will be genuine, lasting, and total peace in that part of the world.
The key to peace and stability in that part of the world, however, rests on one ingredient, and that is the willingness to provide verification. Among the people and groups in those lands the level of distrust is so high that you cannot restore confidence unless there is verification. You will recall, sir, that the Government of Nicaragua, the Sandinista Government, celebrated the inauguration of its Constitution last January. The next day it withdrew that Constitution and declared a state of emergency. It in fact withdrew all of the major provisions for civil and human rights in that country.

August 18, 1987
Adjournment Debate
I have with me a copy of that Constitution provided to me by the embassy here and I note Article 185:
The President of the Republic may suspend, within part or all of the
national territory, the rights and guarantees consecrated in this Constitution in
case of war or when demanded by national security, economic conditions or a
national catastrophe.
It goes on in the next article to indicate certain sections of the Constitution which cannot be suspended. For example, Article 33(2.1), which says that you cannot arbitrarily be detained or imprisoned. However, Article 33(2.2) can be suspended and that article says:
To be brought before a competent legal authority within 72 hours.
That is, every citizen of Nicaragua has the right to be brought before a judge or competent legal authority within 72 hours.
For years we heard about the terrors of the Somoza regime, and we understand that, and the terror of its El Chipote prison. Now we have the shocking news that the Sandinista Government is using that very same installation and denying the right to be heard before a competent legal authority. We met with mothers and wives of political prisoners in Nicaragua. We have a right to be concerned about the level of rights being respected in that country.
My question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs was simply whether he would corroborate the news that 1 had received, that the President of the Conservative Party had been apprehended and that the Party had been banned. There must be some truth to it because when we were there at a conference, we tried to organize a meeting of the opposition Party leaders and were prohibited from meeting with those people within the conference centre. We had to find a room in the hotel to do that.
I come back to my original point. We have now sent two Canadian officials there to provide Canadian aid in bringing about peace. I welcome that. I think we have taken a good initiative. I hope that Canada will do its part together with other nations which are interested in a secure and lasting peace there, that we will provide those means necessary to bring verification to any agreement so that the Cuban, Soviet and Contra troops all become disarmed, so that the people do not have to fear militarization, and that a lasting, just and secure peace can exist for the people of Nicaragua and the surrounding countries. 1 hope that we will provide the verification which will give everyone the confidence that that will be a just peace.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL. AFFAIRS-NICARAGUA-REPORTED BANNING OF CONSERVATIVE PARTY-ACCESS TO POLITICAL PRISONERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my honourable colleague asked his question on June 5, 1987. The Canadian Embassy in Costa Rica has since investigated the allegations made by the Honourable Member about human rights abuses in Nicaragua. The opposition leader to whom he referred is Mr. Maurio Rappaciolli, the leader of the Conservative Party of Nicaragua. Members of his party have
confirmed that neither their leader nor other members were detained or put under house arrest at the time of the IPU meeting.
The Conservative Party of that country was not included among the opposition parties which met IPU delegates because it has no members in the National Assembly, having boycotted the 1984 elections.
The Party attempted to organize a demonstration during the IPU meeting but was unable to do so because State Security agents surrounded its headquarters. The Party has not been banned and there appears to be no legal mechanism for doing so because it is not an officially recognized political party. This does not prevent it carrying out political activities subject to the restrictions which apply to all political parties. For instance, they cannot hold outdoor meetings without prior permission.
The International Committee of the Red Cross has confirmed that its representatives are denied access to the prisoners held in El Chipote because they are political prisoners held by the Ministry for the Interior under administrative detention. The International Committee is given full access to political prisoners once they have been brought before the courts and moved into the national penitentiary system.
The International Committee is denied access to political prisoners who are being held under administrative detention while their cases are investigated. Under the provisions of the state of emergency, there is no limit to the time prisoners can be held in this way.
Although no reliable figures are available, President Ortega said in May 1987 that there were 8,000 to 10,000 prisoners in Nicaragua of whom 60 per cent were common criminals, which presumably means that the other 3,200 to 4,000 are political prisoners. Other independent estimates range from 4,000 to 10,000.
Canada remains concerned by continuing breaches of human and civil rights in Nicaragua, especially instances of arbitrary arrest and harrassment of the churches, opposition groups, the press and trade unions. These concerns have been made known to the Nicaraguan Government on many occasions.
Canada welcomes the fact that the Central American peace plan signed in Guatemala City on August 7 by the five regional Presidents includes a commitment to representative and pluralist democratic systems of government in all countries in the region. We hope that the implementation of the peace plan will result in the lifting of the state of emergency in Nicaragua and the removal of the current restrictions on the press and opposition groups. We urge the Nicaraguan Government to fulfill the original goals of the revolution which have recently been reaffirmed in the Constitution. These goals include political pluralism, a mixed economy and nonintervention in the affairs of other states.
August 18, 1987

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT-RETRAINING OF LAID-OFFOLDER WORKERS. REQUEST FOR MINISTERIAL COMMITMENT
EMPLOYMENT-RETRAINING OF LAID-OFFOLDER WORKERS. REQUEST FOR MINISTERIAL COMMITMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) when the Government would implement the program for the adjustment of older workers that it had announced 18 months ago. The Minister said that he was negotiating with the provinces.
While the Labour Adjustment Benefit Program that was introduced by the previous Government was not totally adequate, it did something for older workers. That has been phased out and we now face a vacuum while the federal Government is negotiating with the provinces. This is a disaster for people between the ages of 54 and 65, who are left without any benefits through no fault of their own, but because plants have closed down.
We must consider a program to fill the vacuum that has been left by the phasing out of the Labour Adjustment Benefit Program. Last year, some $91 million was spent on the Labour Adjustment Benefit Program. That amount has been reduced to $82 million this year.
People in my riding of Hamilton Mountain are being laid off because of the closure of Firestone and Otis Elevator. They will be left to fall through the cracks, with nothing for them. Also, if there is no program from which older workers can quickly benefit, their situation will deteriorate more rapidly. They can adjust very well to new skill training and will enter a new job situation. However, if they are left to fall through the cracks, there will be a lot of domestic pressures and human misery.
The Minister's response that he is negotiating with the provinces is inadequate. Canadians were told 18 months ago that another program would be established. That still has not taken place, which is grossly unfair and certainly does not fulfil a promise. People 54 years old and over in my riding, as well as in others, are the ones who are suffering severely. Not only are they suffering, but their families are suffering as well.
It is not right that people who have contributed to this society by being responsible workers and taking part in this economy should be allowed to fall through the cracks. It is not fair that they should be told to wait for a couple of politicians to negotiate their welfare, which is basically what is happening.
The negotiations with the provinces are taking place behind closed doors. No one knows what is happening. The Minister responds by saying that these people will be looked after when the provinces and the federal Government get on board. The federal Government has a responsibility. It has always paid 100 cent dollars for these kinds of programs and has no right to phase one out if it is not being replaced by another, and if it has not done the negotiations before it is replaced.

When this government took office in September 1984, there was the LAB program, which provided adjustment assistance to laid-off older workers and was due to expire in August 1985. There were 4,200 older workers receiving benefits under this program, total payments being about $42.2 million.

We also extended the LAB designations for the communities of Gagnon, Fermont, Port-Cartier, Sept-Iles, Schefferville, Labrador City, Wabush, Asbestos and Thetford Mines.

The results of these initiatives, Mr. Speaker, have been to greatly increase the federal government's assistance for older

workers. Over 9,000 older workers are currently receiving adjustment benefits and expenditures are expected to reach $96 million this year.
